In Genesis: Jacob's family, a shepherding household descended through Leah, Zilpah, Rachel and Bilhah; sixty-six direct offspring entered Egypt, with Joseph's two Egypt-born sons making seventy, planning to settle in Goshen. In Genesis: consists_of sons of Jacob [blessed each according to his own blessing] The twelve tribes of Israel are identified as the sons Jacob has just addressed, each described in his own pronouncement. In Exodus, the Israelites are the LORD's firstborn people, rescued from Egypt, covenanted at Sinai, and repeatedly failing in obedience. In Exodus, the children of Israel are the LORD's rescued people, brought from Egypt into covenant and worship. In Exodus: The baby is identified as one of the Hebrews' children, and Hebrew women are the source of a possible nurse. In Leviticus, the children of Israel are the LORD's holy people, instructed in sacrifice, purity, justice, and covenant obedience. In Leviticus: offers young bull [sin offering when the sin becomes known] If the whole congregation sins and the matter is hidden from the assembly, then once the sin is known the assembly must offer a young bull as a sin offering. In Numbers: The Israelites are the people promised the land, each tribe sending a spy.

In Numbers, the children of Israel are the LORD's organized wilderness people, repeatedly complaining yet guided, judged, and blessed. In Deuteronomy, Israel is the LORD's chosen covenant people, commanded to obey him despite their rebelliousness. In Deuteronomy: The Israelites are the addressees of Moses, witnesses of the LORD's signs in Egypt, the Red Sea, and the wilderness. In Deuteronomy: Israel is the covenant community and people of the LORD, also the land they inhabit. In Deuteronomy: The LORD's assembly is closed to the emasculated, to those born of a forbidden union, and to Ammonites and Moabites, with the restriction lasting to the tenth generation. In The Book of Joshua: possesses hill country of Ephraim [too narrow for the house of Joseph] Ephraim's territory lay south of Manasseh's along the brook of Kanah, and Ephraim held Tappuah on Manasseh's border and some cities among Manasseh's cities. In The Book of Joshua: The children of Ephraim received an inheritance with a defined border according to their families, from Ataroth Addar and upper Beth Horon to the Jordan and the sea. In The Book of Joshua: The children of Israel are the people to whom the LORD gives the land of Canaan, led by Joshua and commanded to fear and worship the LORD forever. In The Book of Joshua: Israel, called the children of Israel, is a covenant people composed of tribes such as Judah and led by Joshua, elders, heads, judges and officers. In The Book of Judges: number_after_first_reduction ten thousand [after twenty-two thousand returned] Of the people with Gideon, twenty-two thousand return home after the proclamation for the fearful, leaving ten thousand. In The Book of Judges, Israel is the people caught in a cycle of apostasy, oppression, repentance, and deliverance. In The Book of Judges: Ephraim is a hill-country region and its people, living alongside Canaanites in Gezer. In The First Book of Samuel: Israel is a people brought out of Egypt by the LORD yet long inclined to forsake him for other gods. In The First Book of Samuel, Israel is the LORD's chosen people, moving from defeat and repentance through monarchy to Saul's collapse. In The Second Book of Samuel: David's people were set under captains and went out in three divisions, but they persuaded David not to go with them, saying he was worth ten thousand of them. In The Second Book of Samuel: Israel is the people of the LORD, a nation redeemed from Egypt and established as God's people forever, and also the land or place the LORD promises to appoint for them so they dwell there, no longer moved or afflicted. In The First Book of Kings: Israel is a people, named from Jacob by the LORD, who is also treated as a land and later a northern kingdom. In The Second Book of Kings: Israel is both a people and a kingdom/land, with Samaria as its capital where kings reigned and an Asherah remained. In 1 Chronicles: is_a great army like God's army [grew as men came daily to David] David's army grew day by day as men came to help him until it was a great army like God's army. In 1 Chronicles: Israel is the people and kingdom of the LORD, described as the offspring of his servant and the children of Jacob, a chosen people made his own forever and redeemed from Egypt. In 1 Chronicles: The assembly hears David's appeal and rejoices as the people give willingly. In The Second Book of Chronicles: Israel is both a people and the land or kingdom they occupy, as presented in 2 Chronicles. In The Second Book of Chronicles: Jehoshaphat went out among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. In The Book of Ezra: Israel is the covenant people, called the children of Israel, whose story here moves from restoration to failure and repentance. In The Book of Ezra: The Jews are the returned captives in Judah and Jerusalem who worship the God of Israel. In The Book of Ezra: The children of the captivity are exiles who came out of Babylon during Artaxerxes' reign. In The Book of Ezra: The returning exiles, children of the province, were people carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar who came back under Zerubbabel's leadership. In The Book of Nehemiah: The children of Israel are God's servants, redeemed by his great power and strong hand, yet they have sinned, dealing very corruptly and not keeping the commandments given to Moses. In The Book of Nehemiah: Nehemiah's poor Jewish brothers suffer famine and crushing debt bondage, mortgaging fields and houses and surrendering children to servitude; Nehemiah, who had redeemed Jews sold to the nations, argues that selling them again would be wrong. In The Book of Nehemiah: Israel is the covenant people whose story is traced from exile to renewed commitment. In Tobit: located_among Gentiles [scattered by God] The children of Israel are told to give thanks to God before the Gentiles, among whom he has scattered them. In Tobit: will_be scattered on the earth [from the good land] Tobit foretells that his kindred will be scattered on the earth from the good land, but God will have mercy, bring them back, and rebuild Jerusalem. In Judith, the children of Israel are the people of Judea who defend their sanctuary, defeat the Assyrians, and return rejoicing. In Esther (Greek): The Jews are a nation scattered among the nations, described by Haman as having laws different from others and disobeying the king's laws. In The First Book of the Maccabees: Israel is the people and land whose fortunes are traced through a period of persecution, resistance, and recovery. In The First Book of the Maccabees: The Jews are a people regarded by the Gentiles as a state without a ruler, yet permitted by Antiochus to coin their own money. In The Second Book of the Maccabees: The Jews appear as a people chosen by the Lord, bound to laws he ordained, who observe the Sabbath and the feast of weeks, yet who are also described as bound by many sins that turned the Lord's eye away. In Psalms: The LORD's people are those who trust him: shown his works' power, given the nations' heritage, granted redemption and an eternal covenant, then likened to immovable Mount Zion, surrounded by the LORD forever. In Psalms: God's people are the LORD's heritage, his own people and the sheep of his pasture, who made them. In Psalms, Israel is God's chosen inheritance and worshiping people, repeatedly delivered, judged, and called to trust and praise him. In Psalms: The LORD's tribes belong to the LORD and go up to Jerusalem according to an ordinance for Israel, ultimately to give thanks to the LORD's name. In Psalms: A group who call the LORD 'our God' look to him like servants watching a master's hand. In Psalms: A group brought back to Zion by the LORD; they feel like dreamers, filled with laughter and singing, and the nations acknowledge the LORD's great deeds for them. In Psalms: Exiled captives in Babylon sit by the rivers weeping for Zion, hang their harps on willows, and ask how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land. In Psalms: is_shepherded_by LORD [as requested in prayer] The LORD's people are described as having the LORD as their strength, and he is a stronghold of salvation to his anointed. In Psalms: The people, speaking as 'we' and 'I', recall that their fathers won the land through God and not their own sword, and they declare they will not trust in their bow. In Psalms: Ephraim is a tribe described as God's helmet and head's defense, yet its bow-armed children turned back in battle and broke God's covenant, so God rejected it and did not choose it. In Psalms: is_rejected_by God [stated in the plea] God's people are described as rejected, broken down, shown hard things, and made to drink wine that makes them stagger. In Psalms: God's worshippers are those he chooses and brings near; though sins overwhelmed them, God atoned for transgressions. In Psalms: Israel, the speaker's people, is tested by God like refined silver. In Psalms: God's people are his flock and inheritance tribe, purchased and redeemed long ago. In Psalms: The sons of Jacob and Joseph are God's people, the sheep of his pasture. In Psalms: God's people, named Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, suffer: fed bread of tears, contended over by neighbors, mocked by enemies. In Psalms: The people have been forgiven their iniquity and had all their sin covered, yet they plead to be turned, relieved of God's indignation, and revived so they may rejoice in him. In The Wisdom of Solomon: A holy people, a blameless seed, delivered by Wisdom from oppressors; she rewarded their toils, guided and sheltered them by day and night, brought them across the Red sea, and they sang praise to God's holy name. In The Wisdom of Solomon: The righteous Israelites crossed a barren desert, withstood enemies, and when thirsty called on God and received water from the rock; chastened in mercy, they learned how the ungodly were tormented in wrath. In The Wisdom of Solomon: is_covered_by God [covered with God's hand] God's people journeyed on a marvelous road, overshadowed by the cloud and covered by God's hand, and passed over with all their army having seen strange marvels. In The Wisdom of Solomon: God's people, called his servants, children, and 'your sons', belong to God even when they sin, because they know his dominion and trust him. In The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus: Israel is the people called by the Lord's name, his portion and firstborn-like inheritance, composed of the tribes of Jacob. In The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus: Jacob's people are a community of Israel whose story is told across the records. In The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus: A disobedient kingdom ruled out of Ephraim after the sovereignty was divided. In The Book of Isaiah: A people who refuse the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son, so a flood will overwhelm them. In The Book of Isaiah: The remnant of the LORD's people, dispersed in Assyria, Egypt and other lands, will be recovered a second time. In The Book of Isaiah, Jacob is the LORD's chosen servant people, judged for sin and promised redemption and a universal purpose. In The Book of Isaiah: The house of Jacob is a people of the LORD, portrayed across three chapters as both cherished and faulted. In The Book of Isaiah: The children of Israel, also called Jacob and Jeshurun, are portrayed as both a people and a servant figure of the LORD. In The Book of Isaiah: The people of Israel are accused of forgetting the God of their salvation and the rock of their strength, planting pleasant plants and foreign seedlings whose harvest flees in grief. In The Book of Isaiah: The people of Jerusalem and Judah act against the Lord in word and deed, openly parading their sin like Sodom. In The Book of Isaiah: A rebellious people, Judah's lying children, make an alliance with Egypt without consulting the LORD, send riches there, trust in horses and flight, and refuse the offered rest. In The Book of Isaiah: My people are a group whose land will be overgrown with thorns and briers after desolation, yet they will afterward dwell in peaceful habitation, safe dwellings, and quiet resting places, despite hail and a leveled city. In The Book of Isaiah: Israel's dispersed sons and daughters are called by the LORD's name and created for his glory. In The Book of Isaiah: The barren woman's children, promised the LORD's Spirit, will outnumber the married wife's children, spread widely, possess nations, resettle desolate cities, and be taught by the LORD, enjoying great peace. In The Book of Isaiah: The LORD's people, who lived in Egypt, were oppressed by the Assyrian and taken away for nothing, mocked by rulers. In The Book of Isaiah: A people whose iniquities separate them from the LORD: their hands are defiled with blood, their lips speak lies, and they hurry to shed innocent blood, lacking the way of peace. In The Book of Isaiah: The addressed people, Israel, are promised restoration: they rebuild ancient ruins and devastated cities while strangers tend their flocks and fields. In The Book of Isaiah: Israel is the LORD's people, whom he redeemed, saved and carried through the sea and wilderness in days of old. In The Book of Isaiah, Israel is a sinful and rebellious nation reduced to a remnant, then promised salvation and restoration. In The Book of Isaiah: Ephraim is a northern people and territory headed by Samaria, whose own head is Remaliah's son. In The Book of Jeremiah: The daughter of the speaker's people is portrayed as deceitful, lying, and disobedient, rejecting the LORD's law and following Baals taught by fathers; the speaker weeps for her slain, and the LORD resolves to melt and test the people. In The Book of Jeremiah, Israel is the LORD's unfaithful covenant people, exiled for sin yet promised gathering and renewal. In The Book of Jeremiah: The LORD's flock, scattered into many countries by its shepherds and misled by prophets' false dreams and lies, is promised regathering of its remnant to their folds, where it will be fruitful and multiply. In The Book of Jeremiah: Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon, Edom and other countries hear Babylon's king left a remnant under Gedaliah, return to Judah and Gedaliah at Mizpah, and gather abundant wine and summer fruits. In The Book of Jeremiah, the people of Judah and Jerusalem are a rebellious community judged, scattered, and deprived because they reject the LORD. In The Lamentations of Jeremiah: Israel is a group whose beauty the Lord casts from heaven to earth; in fierce anger he cuts off its horn, swallows it and its palaces, and acts as its enemy. In The Lamentations of Jeremiah: has_dwellings swallowed up [by the Lord without pity] All the dwellings of Jacob are swallowed up without pity, and the Lord burns up Jacob like a flaming fire that devours all around. In The Lamentations of Jeremiah, the speakers are a ruined community confessing sin, mourning exile, and asking the LORD for renewal. In The Lamentations of Jeremiah: The people of Jerusalem, starving and sighing, trade their treasures for bread; priests and elders perish seeking food, princes weaken like pasture-less deer, and young men and virgins are crushed and taken into captivity. In Baruch: Exiles living by the river Sud serve Nabuchodonosor yet remain under the Lord's wrath for their sin; they hear the book, weep, fast, pray, send collected money to Jerusalem, and confess their sin. In Baruch, Israel is God's sinful and exiled people, confessing their disobedience and awaiting restoration in God's glory. In The Book of Ezekiel, the house of Israel is a rebellious people judged for idolatry and promised a new heart, spirit, and land. In The Book of Ezekiel: is_a audience of the parable [told to utter a parable to them] The rebellious house is the audience of the cauldron parable that Ezekiel is told to utter. In The Book of Ezekiel: belongs_to the LORD [my sheep, the sheep of my pasture] The sheep were scattered over the mountains and the whole earth for lack of a shepherd and became prey and food for the animals of the field. In The Book of Ezekiel, Israel is the LORD's rebellious covenant people and land, scattered in judgment and restored to secure possession. In The Book of Ezekiel: The people of the land are worshipers who bow at the inner court's east gate door on Sabbaths and new moons; at appointed feasts they enter by the north or south gate and exit by the opposite, walking straight, with the prince among them. In The Book of Ezekiel: The tribes each receive one portion running east to west, and those who labor in the city out of all the tribes cultivate the city's land. In The Book of Ezekiel: The exiles are Ezekiel's brothers and relatives, the whole house of Israel, told by Jerusalem's inhabitants to stay far from the LORD. In The Book of Ezekiel: will_be_unable_to_be_saved_by silver and gold [in the day of the LORD's wrath] The inhabitants are warned that their doom has come, and they are to be judged according to their ways. In Daniel (Greek): Israel is a people called by God's name who, having transgressed his law and disobeyed the prophets, now lie under the curse and oath of Moses' law, scattered through the countries where God drove them, bearing confusion of face. In Daniel (Greek): has_fate delivered [everyone found written in the book] Daniel's people are said to be delivered at the time of trouble, everyone who is found written in the book. In Daniel (Greek): believes two elders [initially trusted them as elders and judges] The people assemble at Joakim's house and believe the elders' testimony, condemning Susanna to death. In The Book of Hosea, Israel is the LORD's adulterous and idolatrous people, judged and promised restoration. In The Book of Hosea: The children are told to say 'My people' and 'My loved one' to their brothers and sisters, and to contend with their mother. In The Book of Hosea: The children of Israel are loved by the LORD despite turning to other gods and loving cakes of raisins. In The Book of Hosea, Ephraim is the unfaithful people judged by the LORD yet promised mercy and restoration. In The Book of Joel: is_heritage_of LORD [his people and heritage] Israel is called the LORD's people and heritage, whom the nations scattered and whose land they divided. In The Book of Joel: The children of Zion, the LORD's heritage, are summoned to tremble and assemble, from elders to nursing children, as priests plead against reproach among nations; the LORD pities them, promises satisfaction, and affirms they will know he is among Israel. In The Book of Amos, Israel is the LORD's chosen but oppressive people, judged for injustice and promised a remnant's restoration. In The Book of Amos: The house of Israel is a collective people, lamented as fallen and called small, whose fate unfolds across three chapters. In The Book of Obadiah: Jacob is Edom's brother, against whom Edom committed violence, and whose Jerusalem and children of Judah suffered disaster and plunder. In The Book of Micah: The LORD's people, treated as a group, are first accused of acting as an enemy: stripping passersby returning from battle, driving women from their pleasant houses, and taking blessing from children. In The Book of Micah: Jacob, the house of Israel, is a collective addressed in judgment: its disobedience, tied to Samaria, justifies coming judgment; it is questioned about the LORD's anger, promised full assembly, and its heads are summoned to know justice as its sin is declared. In The Book of Micah: Israel is the LORD's people, portrayed as a flock and heritage dwelling by themselves in a forest, and as a land. In Habakkuk: The LORD goes out for the salvation of his people and his anointed. In The Book of Zephaniah: has a remnant free of iniquity and lies [will feed, lie down, and be unafraid] The remnant of Israel is promised that it will not do iniquity or speak lies, no deceitful tongue will be found in its mouth, and it will feed and lie down with no one making it ... In The Book of Zechariah: inherits peace, fruit, increase and dew [granted by the LORD of Armies] The remnant is told that its present marvel is not too marvelous for the LORD, and that he will no longer treat it as in the former days of no wages, no peace, and strife with neighbors. In The Book of Zechariah: is_like mighty man [future state; heart rejoices as through wine] Ephraim will be like a mighty man, and their heart will rejoice as with wine. In The Book of Zechariah: The returning exiles are a people promised redemption: the LORD will gather them from Egypt and Assyria, where they were sown among peoples and remember him. In The Book of Zechariah: is_treated_by_buyers buyers and sellers of the flock [buyers slaughter them without punishment] The flock is slaughtered by buyers who go unpunished and sold by sellers who thank the LORD for their riches, while its own shepherds don't pity it. In The Book of Malachi: Israel is addressed by the LORD through Malachi and told that he has loved them, though they ask how. In The Book of Malachi: The people, called the sons of Jacob, are not consumed because the LORD does not change, though they have turned from his ordinances since the days of their fathers. In The Gospel According to Matthew: is_described_as lost sheep [destination of the disciples' mission] The house of Israel is described as lost sheep, and the disciples are sent only to it, not to Gentiles or Samaritan cities. In The Gospel According to John: The Jews appear in these records as a collective antagonist group whose relationship with Jesus moves from questioning and misunderstanding to hostility and finally to delivering him for execution. In The Acts of the Apostles: Paul's sermon recounts Israel's history: chosen fathers, deliverance from Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, the conquest of Canaan, judges, and the kings Saul and David. In The Acts of the Apostles: The Hebrews are the subject of the Hellenists' complaint that the Hellenist widows are neglected in the daily service. In The Acts of the Apostles: The Jews appear as a recurring body opposing Paul across his ministry. In The Acts of the Apostles: contended_with Peter [over eating with uncircumcised men] Those of the circumcision contend with Peter in Jerusalem, objecting that he went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them. In The Acts of the Apostles: Unbelieving Jews in Iconium stir up the Gentiles against the brothers and join in a plot to mistreat and stone the apostles. In The Acts of the Apostles: The Jews are a group made up of twelve tribes who hold a hope in the promise God made to their fathers. In The Acts of the Apostles: The men of Israel are the temple crowd, heirs of God's covenant with the fathers. In Paul’s Letter to the Romans: Jews are a group addressed as bearing the name, resting on the law, and glorying in God, yet charged with failing to practice what they teach, causing God's name to be blasphemed among Gentiles. In Paul’s Letter to the Romans: Israel is a people privileged with adoption, glory, covenants, the giving of the law, service, promises and the fathers, and the line from which Christ came according to the flesh. In 2 Corinthians: has_state hardened minds The children of Israel could not look steadily at Moses' face because of its glory. In Paul’s Letter to the Galatians: Paul says that he and Peter are Jews by nature and not Gentile sinners, yet they believed in Christ Jesus to be justified by faith and not by works of the law. In 1 Thessalonians: The Jews are portrayed as a group who killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, displeased God, and opposed all men. In The Letter to the Hebrews: The house of Israel, with Judah, failed to continue in the first covenant and was disregarded by the Lord, who then promises a new covenant: laws written on hearts, becoming his people, all knowing him. In Revelation: belongs_to God [called 'my people' by a voice from heaven] A voice from heaven calls them to come out of Babylon so that they have no participation in her sins and do not receive her plagues. In Revelation: The children of Israel are a people made up of twelve tribes: Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin. In Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara): Children of Israel receive Allah’s covenant and Scripture through Moses, yet worship the calf, seek a king to fight in Allah’s way, and repeatedly turn away, break covenants, and conceal or disbelieve truth. In Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara): Jews are described as denying that Christians follow anything true, refusing to be pleased with Muhammad unless he follows their creed, and being told they cannot properly claim Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, or the tribes. In Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan): receive the Torah [before the Gospel] Jesus is sent as a messenger to the Children of Israel with signs from Allah. In Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa): The Jews are a group described through acts of disbelief, wrongdoing, and opposition to Allah’s way. In Surah 5: The Table (Al-Maaida): Jews are portrayed as a group identified with the Children of Israel and an old covenant. In Surah 5: The Table (Al-Maaida): The Children of Israel are a group that received Allah's covenant, twelve chieftains, prophets, guidance, and the law of retaliation. In Surah 7: The Heights (Al-A'raaf): Children of Israel, led by Moses, are oppressed then delivered across the sea, receive provision and inheritance, divide into twelve tribes, yet some disobey, worship the calf, and break the covenant. In Surah 10: Jonas (Yunus): The Children of Israel were brought across the sea and given a fixed abode and good things. In Surah 17: The Night Journey (Al-Israa): The Children of Israel are given guidance and warned that they will work corruption in the earth twice. In Surah 20: Taa-Haa: The Children of Israel are delivered from Pharaoh, given a covenant, and provided manna and quails. In Surah 26: The Poets (Ash-Shu'araa): The Children of Israel are enslaved by Pharaoh, are ordered to be released, leave by night with Moses, and are saved when the sea parts. In Surah 28: The Stories (Al-Qasas): The Israelites are represented in this unit as the oppressed tribe among Pharaoh’s people whose sons were killed and women spared. In Surah 32: The Prostration (As-Sajda): The Children of Israel received the Scripture given to Moses. In Surah 43: Ornaments of gold (Az-Zukhruf): Jesus was made a pattern for the Children of Israel. They are mentioned in connection with the favour bestowed upon him. In Surah 44: The Smoke (Ad-Dukhaan): The Children of Israel were delivered from the shameful doom and from Pharaoh. In Surah 61: The Ranks (As-Saff): Jesus son of Mary was sent as Allah's messenger to the Children of Israel. In Surah 62: Friday (Al-Jumu'a): The Jews are described as being entrusted with the Law of Moses but not applying it, like an ass carrying books.

The chapter lists the descendants of Jacob through Leah (thirty-three), Zilpah (sixteen), Rachel (fourteen), and Bilhah (seven), including sons, grandsons, and daughters. Those who came into Egypt were sixty-six direct offspring, and with Joseph's two sons born in Egypt, the house of Jacob numbered seventy.

Israelites in Exodus

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israelites first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Israelites, also called the children of Israel, are a numerous people who belong to the LORD, described as his son and firstborn. The records open with their bondage in Egypt, where Egyptians and taskmasters oppress them. They sigh and cry out, and God hears, remembering his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He promises to bring them to a good and large land. Their labor worsens when they must gather their own straw yet still meet the same brick quota, and their officers are beaten when it falls short. When Aaron speaks and performs the signs, they believe, and on hearing that the LORD has seen their affliction they bow and worship. They are spared the plagues that strike Egypt: none of their livestock dies, and no hail falls in Goshen, where they live. The LORD brings them out of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand. In the wilderness they gather around Moses to have disputes judged, and later are judged by appointed rulers. At the mountain they receive the commandments, including having no other gods before the LORD and honoring parents. Seeing the thunder, lightning, and smoke, they tremble, stay at a distance, and ask Moses to speak to them in place of God. They then accept the covenant, promising with one voice to do and obey all the LORD's words, and Moses sprinkles them with blood. The arc turns when Moses is delayed: they demand gods from Aaron, give up their gold, and worship a molded calf. Moses destroys the calf, about three thousand die, and the LORD strikes them. The LORD calls them stiff-necked and says he will not go up among them. They mourn and strip off their jewelry at his command. By the end they watch Moses go to the Tent and worship when the pillar of cloud descends. Overall, they are a chosen, rescued, and covenanted people whose fear, obedience, and worship alternate with serious failure.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 2

After the king of Egypt dies, the children of Israel sigh and cry out because of their bondage, and their cry rises to God. God hears their groaning, sees them, and remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Chapter 3

The Israelites, called God's people and the children of Israel, are afflicted by taskmasters in Egypt, and their cry has reached God. God promises to bring them out to a good and large land. Their elders will listen to Moses, and the people will ask for silver, gold, and clothing from the Egyptians.

Chapter 4

The Israelites are called the LORD's son, his firstborn, whom Pharaoh is to let go to serve him. Moses worries they will not believe him, but when Aaron speaks and does the signs, they believe. On hearing that the LORD had visited them and seen their affliction, they bow their heads and worship.

Chapter 5

The Israelites are told to gather their own straw and are scattered throughout Egypt to find stubble, while still required to produce the same number of bricks. Their workload becomes heavier, and their officers are beaten when the quota falls short.

Chapter 9

The Israelites, called the children of Israel, are spared the livestock pestilence, as not one of their livestock dies. No hail falls in Goshen, where they live. Pharaoh still does not let them go.

Chapter 18

The people stand around Moses from morning to evening as he judges, coming to him to inquire of God and to have matters settled between a man and his neighbor. After the reorganization they are judged by appointed rulers at all times, and Jethro says they will go to their place in peace.

Chapter 20

The people are addressed with the commandments and perceive the thunderings, lightnings, trumpet sound, and smoking mountain, which makes them tremble and stay at a distance. They ask Moses to speak with them instead of God, fearing they will die, and are told they have seen that God talked with them from heaven.

Chapter 24

The people hear Moses relay the LORD's words and ordinances and answer with one voice that they will do all that he has spoken. After the book of the covenant is read, they promise to do it and be obedient, and Moses sprinkles them with blood. They are not to go up the mountain, and they see the LORD's glory as devouring fire on its top.

Chapter 32

The people, seeing Moses delayed, demand gods from Aaron, give up their gold earrings, and worship the molded calf with offerings, eating, drinking, and play. Moses burns the calf, grinds it, and makes them drink it, and about three thousand of them die. Moses calls their act a great sin, and the LORD strikes them for it.

Chapter 33

The Israelites are called a stiff-necked people and hear the evil news that the LORD will not go up among them. They mourn, put on no jewelry, and strip off their jewelry from Mount Horeb onward at the LORD's command. When Moses goes to the Tent, they rise and watch him from their tent doors, and when the pillar of cloud descends they worship.

children of Israel in Exodus

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where children of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The children of Israel are a people descended from the sons of Israel, including Reuben, who came into Egypt numbering seventy souls. They became fruitful, mighty and so numerous that the land was filled with them, and the Egyptians, who held them in bondage, came to dread them. They are called the LORD's people and armies, dwelling in Goshen, which the LORD set apart from the Egyptians; they had light in their dwellings during the darkness. Their central purpose is to serve the LORD, and Moses and Aaron demand their release. After 430 years in Egypt, they keep the Passover and leave in haste in the month Abib, about 600,000 men on foot besides children, armed, plundering the Egyptians, and encamping at Etham. They pass through the sea on dry ground, see the Egyptians dead, and believe in the LORD and Moses. In the wilderness they repeatedly murmur and quarrel over water and food, yet receive manna for forty years, water from the rock, and victory over Amalek at Rephidim. In the third month they reach the wilderness of Sinai and camp before the mountain, answering together that they will do all the LORD has spoken. They are offered status as his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, conditional on obeying his voice and keeping his covenant. They receive laws: honest dealing, Sabbath and feasts (unleavened bread, weeks, harvest), redemption of the firstborn, no covenants with or bowing to other gods, and the half-shekel ransom. Moses calls them a stiff-necked people and asks pardon for them. Their names are borne on the priestly ephod and breastplate, and the LORD promises to dwell among them. They bring such abundant willing offerings for the sanctuary that Moses restrains them, then build the tabernacle according to all the LORD commanded. The account ends with them travelling only when the cloud lifts from the tabernacle, seeing the cloud by day and fire by night.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

26 sections; each heading opens the text

Exodus / Chapter 1

The sons of Israel who came into Egypt with Jacob are named, totaling seventy souls. After Joseph and his generation died, they grew exceedingly numerous and mighty, and the land was filled with them. Despite affliction they kept multiplying and spreading out, and the Egyptians came to dread them.

Chapter 6

The children of Israel are promised redemption from Egyptian burdens, adoption as the LORD's people, and the land sworn to the patriarchs. They do not listen to Moses because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage. The chapter lists the family heads of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.

Chapter 7

The children of Israel are called the LORD's armies and his people, whom he will bring out of Egypt by great judgments. Moses and Aaron are to demand Pharaoh let them go to serve the LORD in the wilderness.

Chapter 8

The LORD's people are the ones Pharaoh is told to let go so they may serve him, and Moses says they will go three days' journey into the wilderness to sacrifice. Their land of Goshen is set apart from the flies as a division between them and Pharaoh's people.

Chapter 10

The children of Israel are the people Moses demands be released to serve the LORD, with young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. During the three days of darkness all of them have light in their dwellings, but Pharaoh does not let them go.

Chapter 11

The people of Israel are to ask their neighbors for jewels of silver and gold and will be thrust out of Egypt. Not even a dog will bark against them or their animals, showing the LORD's distinction between them and the Egyptians, yet Pharaoh does not let them go.

Chapter 12

The children of Israel are commanded to keep the Passover, eat unleavened bread for seven days, and observe these ordinances forever, and they do as the LORD commanded. They plunder the Egyptians, leave Egypt in haste from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot besides children, and are brought out by their armies.

Chapter 13

The children of Israel are told to remember the day they left Egypt, keep seven days of unleavened bread, and redeem their firstborn sons and donkeys once in the promised land. They go up armed out of Egypt, are led by the wilderness road by the Red Sea, and encamp at Etham after journeying from Succoth.

Chapter 14

The children of Israel obey the instruction to turn back and encamp by the sea, then become very afraid when the Egyptians approach, cry out to the LORD, and complain to Moses that it would have been better to serve the Egyptians. Told to stand still, they walk through the middle of the sea on dry ground with the waters as a wall on their right and left. They see the Egyptians dead on the shore and come to fear and believe in the LORD and Moses.

Chapter 15

The children of Israel sing with Moses and walk on dry land through the middle of the sea. In the wilderness they find no water for three days, murmur against Moses at Marah, are tested by the LORD, and then encamp at Elim by twelve springs and seventy palm trees.

Chapter 16

The children of Israel reach the wilderness of Sin and murmur against Moses and Aaron, longing for the meat pots of Egypt. They gather manna each according to his eating, with some disobeying by leaving it overnight or going out on the Sabbath to gather. They rest on the seventh day and eat manna for forty years until they reach the borders of Canaan.

Chapter 17

The children of Israel travel to Rephidim, find no water, and quarrel with and murmur against Moses, testing the LORD by asking whether he is among them. They drink water from the rock, and then fight Amalek, prevailing or not depending on whether Moses' hand is raised, until Joshua defeats Amalek.

Chapter 18

Israel is described as the people the LORD delivered out of Egypt, and Moses recounts to Jethro the hardships that came upon them on the way. Aaron and the elders of Israel eat bread with Jethro before God, and Moses chooses able men out of all Israel to be heads over the people.

Chapter 19

The children of Israel come to the wilderness of Sinai from Rephidim and camp before the mountain. They answer together that they will do all the LORD has spoken, then wash their garments and prepare for three days. On the third day they tremble at the thunder, lightning and trumpet, stand at the lower part of the mountain, and are forbidden on pain of death to touch it or break through to the LORD.

Chapter 23

The Israelites are commanded to give honest testimony, treat the poor, enemies, and aliens fairly, keep the sabbatical year and Sabbath, and observe three feasts. They are told to obey the angel, avoid other gods, and make no covenant with the land's inhabitants, and are promised a border from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines.

Chapter 25

The children of Israel are to bring an offering for the LORD, taken from everyone whose heart makes him willing. They are to make the sanctuary and its furnishings, and the LORD will give commands for them from the mercy seat.

Chapter 27

The children of Israel are to be commanded to bring pure olive oil beaten for the light so that a lamp burns continually. The lamp's upkeep by Aaron and his sons is a statute forever on their behalf.

Chapter 28

The children of Israel are the group from whom Aaron and his sons are brought near to serve as priests. Their names are engraved in birth order on the two onyx stones on the ephod's shoulders and on the twelve breastplate stones for the twelve tribes. Aaron bears these names and their judgment before the LORD as a memorial, and their holy gifts are made acceptable through the plate on his forehead.

Chapter 29

The children of Israel are to provide the wave offering portions from their peace offerings to Aaron and his sons as their portion forever. The LORD promises to meet them at the Tent of Meeting, sanctify the place by his glory, and dwell among them as their God. They will know he is the LORD who brought them out of Egypt.

Chapter 30

The children of Israel are to give a half-shekel ransom for each person aged twenty and over when counted, with rich and poor giving the same, to avoid plague. Moses is to tell them that the holy anointing oil is holy throughout their generations and must not be copied, nor the incense made for themselves.

Chapter 31

The children of Israel are to be told by Moses to keep the LORD's Sabbaths throughout their generations as a sign and a perpetual covenant. Anyone among them who works on the Sabbath is to be put to death and cut off from the people.

Chapter 34

Israel is described as a stiff-necked people for whom Moses asks pardon and to be taken as the LORD's inheritance. They receive commands to destroy the idolatrous objects of the land, avoid covenants and intermarriage with its inhabitants, and keep the feasts and Sabbath. They fear Moses' shining face, then draw near to hear the commandments.

Chapter 35

The children of Israel are gathered and told to keep the Sabbath and to bring a willing offering. They respond, men and women alike, bringing jewelry, fabrics, skins, metals, wood, spices, oil, and stones as a free will offering for the work.

Chapter 36

The children of Israel bring offerings for the sanctuary work, continuing with free will offerings every morning. They bring so much that they are restrained by Moses' proclamation, since what they had was sufficient and too much.

Chapter 39

The children of Israel make the garments and all the tabernacle work according to all that the LORD commanded Moses. Their names are engraved on the onyx stones of the ephod and on the twelve stones of the breastplate, and they bring the finished work to Moses and receive his blessing.

Chapter 40

The children of Israel travel onward throughout all their journeys only when the cloud is taken up from the tabernacle, and do not move until the day it lifts. They see the cloud by day and the fire in it by night.

children of Israel in Leviticus

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where children of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The children of Israel are the people addressed by the LORD through Moses, who previously lived as foreigners in Egypt and are now being brought to Canaan, a land they will inherit as promised. They are called the LORD's people and servants, set apart as his own, and commanded above all to be holy because the LORD is holy. The records open with rules for offerings: livestock from herd or flock, peace offerings with portions for the priests, and a congregation that stands before the LORD, is blessed by Aaron and Moses, and falls on its face when fire consumes the offering. Rules follow on clean and unclean animals, bodily discharges and uncleanness, and the Day of Atonement, when two goats carry away sins and the people afflict their souls and do no work. Sacrifices must be brought to the Tent of Meeting, blood must not be eaten, and sacrifice to goat idols must stop. Central to the whole is separation from the customs of Egypt, Canaan and the nation being cast out: prohibitions on forbidden sexual relations, Molech, idols, mediums and wizards, with penalties and the warning that the land will vomit out those who commit such abominations. Chapter 19 gathers ethical commands: keep Sabbaths, respect mother and father, honor the elderly, revere the sanctuary, leave field corners and gleanings for the poor and foreigner, keep just measures, and love neighbor and stranger as yourself. Later laws cover feasts as holy convocations with rest and shelters remembering the exodus, oil for the lamp and the bread, and the stoning of a blasphemer. In the land they must keep the Sabbath year and Jubilee, deal fairly, redeem relatives' property, lend to the poor without interest, and not treat fellow Israelites harshly or sell them as slaves, since they are the LORD's servants. The account ends with blessing for obedience and severe punishment for rejecting his laws: defeat, scattering among the nations, and fear in enemy lands. Yet if they confess their own and their fathers' iniquity and humble their uncircumcised hearts, the LORD will remember his covenant and not reject them.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

15 sections; each heading opens the text

Leviticus / Chapter 1

The children of Israel are the audience Moses is told to address. They learn that anyone among them who offers an offering to the LORD must give livestock from the herd or the flock.

Chapter 7

The children of Israel are told not to eat the fat of bull, sheep or goat, and not to eat any blood of bird or animal in any dwelling, on penalty of being cut off. They are to bring their peace offerings with their own hands, and give the breast and right thigh to the priests as a portion forever.

Chapter 9

The children of Israel are told to bring a male goat, a calf and a lamb, a bull and a ram, and a meal offering mixed with oil, and the congregation brings these and stands before the LORD. They are blessed by Aaron and by Moses and Aaron, and when they see fire consume the offering on the altar, they shout and fall on their faces.

Chapter 11

The children of Israel receive rules on which animals they may eat and which they must not eat or touch. They are told to avoid making themselves abominable or defiled and to be holy because the LORD, who brought them out of Egypt, is holy.

Chapter 15

The children of Israel are given instructions on how to handle uncleanness from discharges, including washing, bathing, waiting, and offerings. The laws are meant to separate them from their uncleanness so they do not die when they defile the LORD's tabernacle among them.

Chapter 16

The children of Israel supply the two male goats and a ram for the offerings. Their uncleanness, transgressions, and sins are atoned for, and the iniquities are placed on the live goat that carries them away. They are commanded, along with natives and strangers among them, to afflict their souls and do no work on the tenth day of the seventh month.

Chapter 17

The children of Israel are commanded to bring any bull, lamb, or goat they kill to the door of the Tent of Meeting, on penalty of being cut off. They must stop sacrificing to the goat idols, must not eat blood, must pour out and cover the blood of hunted game, and must wash and bathe if they eat what died of itself or was torn by animals.

Chapter 18

The children of Israel are commanded not to act as the people of Egypt, where they lived, or Canaan, where they are being brought, but to keep the LORD's statutes and ordinances. They are given prohibitions on sexual relations and on giving children to Molech, and are warned that doing these abominations will cause the land to vomit them out and lead to being cut off from their people. The commands apply to the native-born and to strangers living among them.

Chapter 19

The whole congregation of the children of Israel is commanded to be holy as the LORD is holy. They receive laws on worship, sacrifice, justice, care for the poor, treatment of neighbors and strangers, and are told to observe all his statutes and ordinances.

Chapter 20

The children of Israel, along with the strangers living among them, are told the penalties for idolatry, cursing parents, adultery, and forbidden sexual relations. They are commanded to sanctify themselves, keep the LORD's statutes and ordinances, distinguish clean from unclean animals, and not walk in the customs of the nation being cast out. They are told they will inherit that land and have been set apart to be the LORD's.

Chapter 22

The children of Israel make the holy things holy to the LORD, and they and the foreigners among them are told to bring offerings that are acceptable. A person who eats a holy thing unwittingly must add a fifth of its value and give it to the priest. They are urged to keep the LORD's commandments and not profane his name.

Chapter 23

The children of Israel are the people commanded to proclaim the feasts as holy convocations, to rest from regular work on them, and to bring the prescribed offerings. They are told to observe the feasts as statutes forever, to leave field corners and gleanings for the poor and foreigner, and to dwell in temporary shelters so that their generations remember the exodus from Egypt.

Chapter 24

The children of Israel are commanded to bring pure olive oil for the lamp, and the bread is an everlasting covenant on their behalf. They hold the blasphemer in custody, and those who heard him lay hands on his head, and the congregation stones him as the LORD commanded.

Chapter 25

The children of Israel are told that when they enter the land they must keep the Sabbath year, count the Jubilee, deal fairly in sales, and not wrong one another. They are commanded to redeem relatives' property, to lend to a poor brother without interest, and not to rule over fellow Israelites harshly. They are called the LORD's servants, so they may not be sold as slaves.

Chapter 26

The Israelites are told that their obedience will bring blessing and their rejection of the LORD's laws will bring severe punishment. If disobedient, they will be defeated, scattered among the nations, and left fearful in enemy lands. If they confess their own and their fathers' iniquity and humble their uncircumcised hearts, the LORD will remember his covenant and not reject them.

Israelites in Numbers

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israelites first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Israelites are the people promised the land, each tribe sending a spy. At Kadesh they hear Caleb's call to conquer alongside the other spies' evil report. Rebellion follows: some join the rebels, the rest flee as the earth swallows them, then the congregation blames Moses and Aaron, and a plague kills 14,700 until Aaron's atonement stops it. Back at Kadesh in Zin they quarrel over water and food, drink from the rock, are refused passage by Edom, and mourn Aaron thirty days at Mount Hor. Finally, with Moses praying for a shepherd, they are told to obey Joshua.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 13

The children of Israel are the people to whom the land is promised, and each of their tribes supplies a spy. At Kadesh the congregation is shown the fruit and hears both Caleb's call to conquer and the other spies' evil report.

Chapter 16

Some Israelites join the rebellion, while the rest are warned to depart from the rebels' tents and flee when the earth swallows them. The next day the congregation complains that Moses and Aaron have killed the LORD's people. A plague then kills 14,700 before Aaron's atonement stops it.

Chapter 20

The Israelites come to the wilderness of Zin and stay at Kadesh, where they quarrel with Moses and Aaron over lack of water and food, wishing they had died. They drink the water from the rock, are refused passage by Edom and turn away, and then come to Mount Hor, where they mourn Aaron for thirty days.

Chapter 27

The congregation witnessed the daughters' plea at the Tent of Meeting. Moses prayed that it not be like sheep without a shepherd, and it was told to obey Joshua, who would lead its going out and coming in.

children of Israel in Numbers

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where children of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The children of Israel, also called Jacob, are the people brought out of Egypt by the LORD's might, organized into tribes and fathers' houses each headed by a prince, and bound to the LORD by command and law. The records open at Sinai, where they are counted at 603,550 fighting men and told to encamp each by his own standard around the Tent of Meeting, at a distance from it. They obey the LORD's commands: putting the unclean outside the camp, keeping Passover in the first month, and traveling or camping by the cloud. The Levites are taken in place of their firstborn to serve and make atonement, and the people may not approach the Tent of Meeting lest they bear sin and die, a fear they voice themselves. They depart Sinai in the second year in ordered tribal divisions. The journey is marked by repeated complaint: weeping for the food of Egypt (fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic), fire at Taberah, plague at Kibroth Hattaavah, then Hazeroth, where they wait for Miriam, and the wilderness of Paran. They wish to return to Egypt, threaten Joshua and Caleb, and are sentenced to wander forty years, with the dead falling in the wilderness. They presume to attack and are beaten to Hormah. They are given offering laws, the red heifer statute (one law for them and the stranger), and are punished with snakes and healed by the bronze serpent. They then defeat Sihon and Og and possess their lands. In the plains of Moab, Balaam cannot curse them: God declares them blessed, a people dwelling alone, strong as a wild ox, like a lioness and lion, with a king among them, no enchantment against them, and a future star and scepter rising from them. Those who bless them are blessed and those who curse them are cursed. Yet at Shittim they join Baal Peor, provoking the LORD's anger and a plague of twenty-four thousand until Phinehas acts. A second census counts 601,730, with none of the earlier generation remaining except Caleb and Joshua. The book closes with festival offerings, vengeance on Midian, Reuben and Gad's pledge, the journey recounted from Egypt under Moses and Aaron, and commands to drive out Canaan's inhabitants, allot the land by lot, give the Levites cities in proportion, appoint cities of refuge, and keep inheritances within tribes.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

28 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 1

The children of Israel are assembled on the first day of the second month and declare their ancestry by families and fathers' houses. They are counted tribe by tribe, totaling 603,550 men of fighting age, and are told to pitch their tents each by his own camp and standard. They do all that the LORD commanded.

Chapter 2

The children of Israel are told to encamp each man by his own standard around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it. They are counted at 603,550 by their fathers' houses and obey, encamping and setting out by their standards, families, and fathers' houses.

Chapter 3

The children of Israel are the people on whose behalf the Levites serve and whose firstborn are replaced by the Levites. Their firstborn males are counted, and the surplus is redeemed with money paid to Aaron and his sons.

Chapter 5

The children of Israel are commanded to put the unclean outside the camp, and they obey exactly as the LORD spoke to Moses. They are also given the rules for restitution and for the jealousy ordeal.

Chapter 6

The children of Israel are the audience for the Nazirite law, which allows any man or woman among them to take the vow. They are also the people to be blessed by Aaron and his sons, who put the LORD's name on them.

Chapter 8

The children of Israel lay their hands on the Levites and, with Moses and Aaron, do to them all the LORD commanded. Their firstborn, both man and animal, belong to the LORD, and the Levites are taken in place of them to serve and make atonement for Israel.

Chapter 9

The children of Israel keep the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day at evening, in the wilderness of Sinai, as the LORD commanded Moses. They are told of the second-month provision and the penalty of being cut off for a clean, non-traveling man who neglects it. They travel or encamp according to the cloud, however long it stays, keeping the LORD's command.

Chapter 10

Israel is instructed in the trumpet signals and then departs the wilderness of Sinai in the second year, tribe by tribe under named army leaders, in the order Judah, Reuben, Ephraim, and Dan. They travel toward the place the LORD said he would give them. They set out from the Mount of the LORD with the ark going before them three days' journey, and they are covered by the cloud by day.

Chapter 11

The people complain and weep for meat, remembering the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt and scorning the manna. The LORD's fire burns among them at Taberah, and after they gather quails greedily, a great plague strikes them and they bury those who lusted at Kibroth Hattaavah before traveling to Hazeroth.

Chapter 14

The children of Israel weep, murmur against Moses and Aaron, wish they had died in Egypt or the wilderness, and propose choosing a leader to return to Egypt. They threaten to stone Joshua and Caleb, then are sentenced to wander forty years. After mourning, they presume to go up the mountain against Moses' warning and are beaten down to Hormah.

Chapter 15

The children of Israel are told what to offer once they enter the land, including the first of their dough as a wave offering. They are given provisions for unwitting sin, and as a congregation they stone the Sabbath breaker outside the camp. They are also told to wear fringes with a blue cord to remember the LORD's commandments and to be holy to their God.

Chapter 17

The children of Israel, through their princes, each give Moses a rod, and afterward each man takes back his own rod when they look at them. They then cry out in fear that they perish and are undone, saying that everyone who approaches the LORD's tabernacle dies.

Chapter 18

The children of Israel give the wave offerings, first fruits, devoted things, and firstborn, and their tithe goes to the Levites. They are forbidden to come near the Tent of Meeting lest they bear sin and die, and the LORD has taken the Levites from among them.

Chapter 19

The children of Israel are told to bring a red heifer without spot or defect that was never yoked. The ashes are kept for their congregation, and the statute is to be perpetual for them and for the stranger living among them.

Chapter 21

Israel vows to destroy the Canaanite cities if the LORD delivers them, and the vow is fulfilled at Hormah. The people complain on the journey and are punished with snakes, then are healed through the bronze serpent, and they sing to the well at Beer. Israel defeats Sihon and Og, possesses their lands, and lives in the cities of the Amorites.

Chapter 22

The children of Israel encamp in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho, having already defeated the Amorites. Moab fears them because they are many, likening them to an ox licking up grass. God tells Balaam that Israel is blessed and must not be cursed.

Chapter 23

Israel, also called Jacob, is described as a people dwelling alone and not listed among the nations, too numerous to count. It is said that the LORD sees no iniquity or perverseness in it, that God brought it out of Egypt with the strength of a wild ox, and that it rises like a lioness and a lion that will not lie down until it eats the prey.

Chapter 24

Israel is seen dwelling according to its tribes, and its tents and dwellings are called goodly. It is described as well watered, brought out of Egypt by God, and as strong as a wild ox, and likened to a lion that no one can rouse. Balaam foretells that a star and scepter from Jacob will crush Moab and the sons of Sheth, make Edom and Seir possessions, and that everyone who blesses Israel is blessed and everyone who curses it is cursed.

Chapter 25

Israel stayed in Shittim, where the people ate and bowed down at sacrifices to the gods of the daughters of Moab and joined themselves to Baal Peor. This brought the LORD's anger and a plague that killed twenty-four thousand, which stopped after Phinehas acted. Israel was spared from being consumed through Phinehas's jealousy.

Chapter 26

The children of Israel are counted by tribe and family, with a total of 601,730 men twenty and older able to go to war. The text says none of those counted earlier at Sinai remained, except Caleb and Joshua. The tribes are to inherit the land by lot according to their numbers.

Chapter 28

The children of Israel are to be commanded, through Moses, to present the LORD's offerings in their due season. They are to offer the continual, Sabbath, monthly and festival offerings, keep holy convocations, and do no regular work on the first and seventh days of unleavened bread and on the day of first fruits.

Chapter 29

The children of Israel are instructed to hold holy convocations, refrain from regular work, and bring the prescribed offerings on the first, tenth, fifteenth and eighth-after-fifteenth days of the seventh month. They are told to offer these in their set feasts in addition to their vows and free will offerings. Moses tells them all that the LORD commanded.

Chapter 31

The children of Israel are to be avenged on Midian, and each tribe supplies a thousand men for the war. They take the plunder and divide it into two halves, with the congregation's half taxed one in fifty for the Levites.

Chapter 32

The children of Israel are the people whose hearts Moses fears Reuben and Gad will discourage from entering the land the LORD gave them. Reuben and Gad promise to go armed before them and not return home until every Israelite has received an inheritance.

Chapter 33

The children of Israel left Egypt by their armies under Moses and Aaron and traveled through many encampments to the plains of Moab. There they camped by the Jordan from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim and were commanded to drive out Canaan's inhabitants and inherit the land by lot.

Chapter 34

The children of Israel are commanded, through Moses, about the land they will enter and inherit. They are told its borders and that it will be allotted by lot to the nine tribes and the half-tribe.

Chapter 35

The children of Israel are commanded to give the Levites cities and pasture lands from their inheritances, with many cities from the larger tribes and few from the smaller. They are also to appoint six cities of refuge, to take no ransom for a murderer, and not to pollute the land.

Chapter 36

The children of Israel are commanded by Moses, according to the LORD's word, that no inheritance may move from tribe to tribe and that each shall keep the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers. The commandments and ordinances are said to have been given to them in the plains of Moab.

Israel in Deuteronomy

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people addressed by Moses in these records: a chosen, holy people of the LORD, descended from the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, grown from seventy persons who went to Egypt into a multitude like the stars, yet described as the fewest of all peoples. Also called Jeshurun, they were servants and slaves under Pharaoh in Egypt, witnessed plagues and wonders, and wandered forty years in the wilderness. The most important theme is covenant: the LORD chose them not for righteousness but by oath to the fathers, and requires them to fear, love, serve and cling to him alone, keep his commandments, and avoid other gods, idolatry, intermarriage and covenants with the nations. Equally prominent is their character as stiff-necked and rebellious from leaving Egypt onward, spared only through Moses' intercession. The account unfolds from Moses' reminders of the journey: refusal at Kadesh, circling Mount Seir, passing Edom, Moab and Ammon peacefully, and defeating Sihon and Og, whose land went to Reubenites, Gadites and half of Manasseh, leaving Israel near Beth Peor. Moses then recalls Horeb, where they feared the fire and voice, and sets out extended commands: destroy pagan worship sites, worship only at the chosen place, avoid blood, tithe, keep the feasts, appoint judges, punish idolatry, obey priests and the coming prophet, care for Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows, cancel debts, and conduct war and civil life justly. Ceremonies on Mounts Ebal and Gerizim and the covenant renewal make them the people of the LORD. Blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience are laid out, along with predictions that they will turn to other gods, be scattered, then return and be restored; they lack a heart to know as yet and are offered a choice of life or death. The law is to be read every seven years, and a song calls them a perverse generation who abandoned the Rock, yet promises compassion. It ends with Moses' blessing: Israel is happy, saved by the LORD, dwelling in safety in a land of grain and new wine, with enemies submitting.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

29 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 1

Israel is addressed by Moses and reminded that the LORD multiplied them like the stars and commanded them to possess the land. At Kadesh they refused to go up, murmured against the LORD, then presumptuously attacked, were beaten by the Amorites, and wept unheard before staying many days in Kadesh.

Chapter 2

Israel circles Mount Seir many days, then obeys the LORD by passing peacefully by Esau's descendants, Moab, and Ammon and buying food and water. After the generation of men of war dies out, Israel offers Sihon peace, is refused, defeats him at Jahaz, destroys his cities, takes livestock and plunder, and stays away from Ammon's land as forbidden.

Chapter 3

The Israelites went up the way to Bashan, defeated Og and his people, took all his cities, and utterly destroyed the inhabitants while taking the livestock and plunder. They took the land from the two Amorite kings between the Arnon and Mount Hermon, and remained in the valley near Beth Peor.

Chapter 4

Israel is addressed as a people who saw the LORD's acts at Baal Peor and heard his voice from the fire at Horeb, and those who stayed faithful are alive. They are called to obey, teach their children, and avoid idolatry, with a warning that disobedience will bring scattering and few survivors among the nations. The text also says they will seek the LORD there, find him, and return, because he chose them and brought them out of Egypt to be his inheritance.

Chapter 5

Israel is addressed as the generation alive today with whom the covenant was made. At Horeb they feared the fire and voice, asked Moses to go near and speak for the LORD, and promised to hear and do what he told them. The LORD approved their words, sent them back to their tents, and they are urged to walk in his way without turning right or left.

Chapter 6

Israel is commanded to hear, love the LORD, keep his words on their hearts, teach them to their children, and not forget him once they are prosperous in the land. They are forbidden to follow other gods or tempt the LORD as at Massah. They are told that observing all the commandments will be righteousness to them.

Chapter 7

The Israelites are addressed as a holy people chosen by the LORD as his own possession, not because they were many but because they were the fewest. They are commanded to destroy the nations, avoid covenants and intermarriage, destroy idolatrous objects, not covet the silver and gold on them, keep the commandments, and not fear the greater nations. If they obey, they will be blessed above all peoples.

Chapter 8

The Israelites are commanded to keep all the commandments, remember the wilderness years, and bless the LORD when they eat and are full in the land. They are warned not to forget him or to credit their own power for their wealth. If they forget him and worship other gods, they will surely perish like the nations destroyed before them.

Chapter 9

Israel is about to cross the Jordan to possess the land, but is told repeatedly that it is a stiff-necked people who have been rebellious since leaving Egypt. They provoked the LORD at Horeb, Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh Barnea, and were spared from destruction only through Moses' intercession.

Chapter 10

Israel traveled from Beeroth Bene Jaakan to Moserah and on to Gudgodah and Jotbathah, and was spared destruction by the LORD. They are told to go in and possess the land sworn to their fathers, and are reminded that the LORD chose them above all peoples. They are commanded to circumcise their hearts, stop being stiff-necked, love the foreigner, and are noted to have grown from seventy persons to a multitude like the stars of the sky.

Chapter 12

The Israelites are commanded to destroy the nations' worship sites, bring their offerings only to the LORD's chosen place, and rejoice there with their households. They may eat meat at home but must not eat blood, must not forsake the Levite, must not imitate the nations' gods, and must neither add to nor take away from the commands.

Chapter 13

Israel is commanded to walk after the LORD, fear him, keep his commandments, obey his voice, serve him, and cling to him. They are told to refuse any enticement to other gods, to carry out the death penalty without pity, and to investigate and destroy any city that turns away. All Israel is meant to hear and fear so that such wickedness is not done again among them.

Chapter 14

The Israelites are told they are children of the LORD and a holy people chosen for his own possession. They are forbidden to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead, to eat abominable things, or to eat what dies of itself. They are commanded to tithe, to eat and rejoice before the LORD, and to care for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

Chapter 15

The Israelites are commanded to cancel debts among themselves every seventh year, to give generously to the poor, and to free Hebrew servants with provisions after six years. They are promised blessing and rule over many nations if they obey. They are also told to dedicate firstborn animals, eat them at the chosen place, and not eat blood.

Chapter 16

The Israelites are commanded to keep Passover, unleavened bread, weeks, and booths, rejoicing with their households, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows. All males appear before the LORD three times a year, giving as able, and they are to remember they were slaves in Egypt. They must also appoint judges, judge justly, and avoid the Asherah and sacred stones so that they may live and inherit the land.

Chapter 17

The people are to inquire diligently into reported idolatry and carry out the stoning at the gates, with the witnesses first and then all the people. They are to take hard cases to the chosen place and obey the verdict, and they will hear and fear and not act presumptuously. When they possess the land and ask for a king like the nations around them, they are told to set over themselves the one the LORD chooses.

Chapter 18

Israel is told to give the priests their due, including first fruits, and not to imitate the abominations of the nations when it enters the land. The people are to be blameless before the LORD, to listen to the coming prophet, and to recognize false prophecy by whether it comes to pass, without fearing the false prophet.

Chapter 20

Israel is addressed as the people going out to battle, told not to fear larger forces with horses and chariots. They are to offer peace to cities, besiege those that refuse, and destroy the peoples of the inherited cities completely. They are to spare fruit trees during sieges.

Chapter 21

Israel is the people the LORD has redeemed and who are to put away innocent blood by doing what is right in his eyes. They are given laws on unsolved killing, captive wives, inheritance, a rebellious son, and burial of the hanged. All Israel is to hear of the rebellious son's punishment and fear.

Chapter 23

The Israelites are commanded in this unit to exclude certain people from the assembly, not to abhor Edomites or Egyptians, to keep their camp clean and holy, and to shelter escaped servants without oppressing them. They are also told to avoid prostitution, not to charge a brother interest (though they may charge a foreigner), to pay their vows, and to limit what they take from a neighbor's vineyard or grain.

Chapter 25

Israel receives laws on judicial beatings capped at forty stripes, the ox not being muzzled, levirate duty, punishment for a woman's act in a fight, and honest weights and measures. It is told that a dead man's name must not be blotted out of Israel, that a refusing brother's house will be named in Israel, and that it must remember and blot out Amalek.

Chapter 26

They are told to bring the first of their fruit in a basket to the chosen place, recite a confession of their history, worship, and rejoice. In the third year they must give the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, and declare their obedience. They declare the LORD to be their God and are declared his own people, called to be a holy people who keep all his commandments.

Chapter 27

Israel is told to cross the Jordan, set up inscribed stones and an altar on Mount Ebal, and hear that today they have become the people of the LORD their God. The tribes are divided between Mounts Gerizim and Ebal, and all the people are to answer 'Amen' to each curse the Levites pronounce.

Chapter 28

The Israelites are told that obeying the LORD's voice and commandments brings them blessing, prosperity, and a position as head and not tail. Disobedience is said to bring curses, defeat, disease, siege, exile, and slavery, until they are left few in number despite having been as many as the stars. They are also charged with not having served the LORD with joy in the midst of abundance.

Chapter 29

Israel, including heads, tribes, elders, officers, men, little ones, wives, and foreigners, stands before the LORD to enter his covenant and oath, by which he establishes them as his people. They are reminded of Egypt, the wilderness, and victories over Sihon and Og, and are told they have not yet been given a heart to know. They are warned that abandoning the covenant for other gods would bring the curses and expulsion from their land.

Chapter 30

The Israelites are told that after the blessing and curse come on them and they are driven among the nations, they will call these to mind, return to the LORD, and obey his voice with all their heart and soul. They are promised restoration and prosperity if they obey. They are given a choice between life and death, and told that turning away to worship other gods will cause them to perish and not prolong their days in the land.

Chapter 31

Israel is told that the LORD will give them the land and that they must obey the law and hear it read every seven years, including women, children and foreigners. The LORD predicts they will prosper, turn to other gods, break the covenant, and suffer evils, and Moses says he knows their rebellion and stiff neck. They are taught the song.

Chapter 32

Israel, called Jacob and Jeshurun, is described as the LORD's portion, found in the wilderness and richly provided for. It grew fat, abandoned the Rock who made it, and is called a perverse and crooked generation, void of counsel. It is threatened with severe judgment but is promised that the LORD will have compassion on his servants and atone for his land and people.

Chapter 33

Israel is the people blessed by Moses, gathered with all its tribes when the LORD was king in Jeshurun. The chapter ends by declaring Israel happy, a people saved by the LORD who dwells in safety in a land of grain and new wine, whose enemies will submit and whose high places it will tread on.
