children of Israel in The Book of Joshua

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where children of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The children of Israel are the people to whom the LORD gives the land of Canaan, led by Joshua and commanded to fear and worship the LORD forever. The records trace their move from promise to settlement. Told to prepare food, they sanctify themselves, follow the ark, and cross the Jordan on dry ground near Jericho while the priests stand in the river. Forty thousand armed men from Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh cross before the LORD. They encamp at Gilgal on the tenth day of the first month, fearing Joshua as they had feared Moses. There they are circumcised at the LORD's command, keep the Passover, and eat the land's produce as the manna ceases. Jericho is shut up because of them; they are warned against taking devoted things, and Rahab and her family are brought out and live among Israel. They are then recorded as having struck the kings east of the Jordan with Moses, possessing the land from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, and the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan with Joshua. The land is divided by lot among nine and a half tribes as the LORD commanded Moses, and the Levites receive only cities with pasture lands, after which the land rests from war. The whole congregation assembles at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting. Three men per tribe survey the land, and the division is finished by borders and lot before the LORD. They give Joshua Timnathserah, which he asked for. They assign cities of refuge for themselves and the alien among them. Finally, hearing of an altar, they gather at Shiloh for war against the eastern tribes, but first send Phinehas and ten princes. Satisfied by the explanation, they bless God and abandon the war.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

11 sections; each heading opens the text

The Book of Joshua / Chapter 1

The children of Israel are the people to whom the LORD is giving the land, and Joshua is to cause them to inherit it. They are told through the officers to prepare food for crossing the Jordan within three days.

Chapter 3

The children of Israel camp at the Jordan, are told to follow the ark at a distance of about two thousand cubits, and are told to sanctify themselves. They then pass over the Jordan on dry ground near Jericho until the whole nation has crossed.

Chapter 4

Israel completed the crossing of the Jordan, hurrying over while the priests stood in the river. Forty thousand armed men from Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh passed over before the LORD to the plains of Jericho. The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and encamped at Gilgal, and they feared Joshua as they had feared Moses.

Chapter 5

The children of Israel are circumcised at the LORD's command, stay in camp until healed, and camp at Gilgal. They keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the plains of Jericho, eat unleavened cakes and parched grain of the land, and no longer receive manna, eating the fruit of Canaan that year.

Chapter 6

The children of Israel are the reason Jericho is tightly shut up. Their camp is warned not to take any devoted thing lest it become accursed and troubled. Rahab and her family are brought out and set outside the camp of Israel, and Rahab lives in the middle of Israel to this day.

Chapter 12

The children of Israel struck the kings east of the Jordan with Moses and possessed their land from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon. They then struck the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan with Joshua, and the land was given to the tribes of Israel as a possession.

Chapter 14

The children of Israel took their inheritances in the land of Canaan, divided by lot among nine tribes and a half-tribe as the LORD commanded Moses. They gave the Levites no portion except cities to dwell in with pasture lands, and the land then had rest from war.

Chapter 18

The whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there. They were told by Joshua to appoint three men from each tribe for surveying the land, and the land was then divided among them by lot.

Chapter 19

The children of Israel finished distributing the land by its borders and gave Joshua the city he asked for, Timnathserah. Their leaders completed the division by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.

Chapter 20

The children of Israel are commanded to assign the cities of refuge and set apart Kedesh, Shechem, Kiriath Arba, Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan. The cities are appointed for all of them and for the alien living among them.

Chapter 22

The children of Israel hear that an altar has been built and gather at Shiloh to go to war against the eastern tribes. They first send Phinehas and ten princes to confront them, citing the iniquity of Peor and Achan's trespass. Satisfied by the explanation, they bless God and abandon the plan for war.

Israel in The Book of Joshua

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel, called the children of Israel, is a covenant people composed of tribes such as Judah and led by Joshua, elders, heads, judges and officers. It is bound to the LORD by covenant and obligated to keep the book of the law of Moses, holding fast to the LORD. Its land in Canaan, a good land stretching from the Jordan to the great sea, is a gift from the LORD, not something it labored for. The records open with Jericho: Israel marches as commanded, shouts at the trumpet, takes the city, and is warned against devoted things. Achan's trespass in taking them makes Israel itself devoted for destruction; it flees before Ai until Achan and his household are found by tribe, family and household, then stoned and burned. Israel then feigns defeat, takes Ai, and gathers at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal to hear the law. At Gibeon it fails to seek the LORD's counsel, is deceived, and spares the Gibeonites because of its oath. It defeats the Amorite coalition, conquers the south, then the northern coalition, and the land rests from war. Remaining peoples such as the Geshurites and Maacathites are not driven out and still live within Israel. The land is allotted by tribe, and Levites receive cities from Israel's inheritance. Israel enjoys rest on every side, with no enemy standing against it. In Joshua's charge, Israel is told to be courageous, keep the law, hold fast to the LORD, and not mingle with the remaining nations, on pain of perishing from the good land. At Shechem the assembled leaders hear the history of the LORD's deliverance, vow repeatedly to serve the LORD, call themselves witnesses against themselves, and agree to put away foreign gods. Israel serves the LORD throughout Joshua's lifetime and that of the elders who outlived him, and buries Joseph's bones at Shechem.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 6

Joshua's people march around Jericho as commanded and stay silent until he tells them to shout. On the seventh day they shout with a great shout at the trumpet sound, go up into the city straight ahead, take it, and destroy all that is in it with the sword. They are warned against taking devoted things, and the metals go into the LORD's treasury.

Chapter 7

Israel, through Achan's trespass, became devoted for destruction and fled before the men of Ai, their hearts melting like water. They were sanctified and brought near by tribe, family, household, and man, then all Israel took part in stoning and burning Achan and his household and raised a heap of stones over him.

Chapter 8

Israel, under Joshua, feigns defeat before Ai, then turns back when the city's smoke rises and kills the men of Ai. They take only the livestock and goods of the city as the LORD commanded. All Israel, including elders, officers, judges, women, little ones, and foreigners, later assembles at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal to hear the law.

Chapter 9

The men of Israel question the Gibeonites' claim, sample their provisions, and do not ask counsel from the LORD. After discovering the ruse, the congregation murmurs against the princes but does not strike the Gibeonites because of the oath sworn by the LORD.

Chapter 10

Israel, led by Joshua, defeated the Amorite coalition at Gibeon and pursued it, then returned in peace to Joshua at Makkedah with none speaking against them. Israel went on to conquer the cities of the south and the surrounding land, then returned to the camp at Gilgal.

Chapter 11

Israel, under Joshua, defeats the northern coalition, strikes the cities with the sword, and takes their plunder and livestock. Israel receives the land as an inheritance by tribes, and the land rests from war.

Chapter 13

Israel is promised that the LORD will drive out the remaining peoples, and its land is to be allocated by inheritance. The children of Israel killed Balaam son of Beor the soothsayer with the sword, but they did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites, who live within Israel to this day.

Chapter 21

The children of Israel give the Levites cities with pasture lands out of their own inheritance, according to the LORD's commandment. They then possess and live in all the land, enjoy rest on every side, and see no enemy stand against them.

Chapter 23

Israel received rest from their enemies and had seen the LORD fight for them, so that no man had stood before them. They are charged to be courageous, keep the law, hold fast to the LORD, and not mingle with the remaining nations. They are warned that disobedience would lead them to perish quickly from the good land.

Chapter 24

Israel's tribes, elders, heads, judges, and officers gather at Shechem and hear the history of the LORD's deliverance. The people repeatedly vow to serve the LORD, declare themselves witnesses against themselves, and agree to put away foreign gods. They serve the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, and they bury Joseph's bones at Shechem.

Israel in The Book of Judges

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people, also called the children of Israel, whose story in these records is a repeating cycle of faithfulness, lapse, oppression, crying out, and deliverance. After Joshua's death they ask the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites. Once strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor instead of driving them out. They then live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, intermarry with them, and forget the LORD. They serve the Baals, Asheroth and Ashtaroth, which provokes the LORD, and they are described as stubborn and as acting more corruptly than their fathers. They served the LORD through the days of Joshua and the elders who outlived him. After that they do evil again and again, and are handed to enemies: Cushan Rishathaim for eight years, Eglon for eighteen, Jabin for twenty, Midian, and the Philistines and Ammonites, with the Philistines holding them forty years. Each time they cry out and are saved by judges or deliverers: Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon and Jephthah. The land has rest for forty and eighty years at different points. Under Midian they are brought very low, hiding in dens, caves and strongholds. After Gideon, whom they asked to rule them, makes an ephod and dies, they turn to the Baals and Baal Berith and show his house no kindness. Tola and Jair lead them for stretches. Later they put away foreign gods, serve the LORD, and assemble at Mizpah. Jephthah recounts how the LORD gave them the Amorite land after Sihon, and they lived in Heshbon three hundred years. The final chapters note that there was no king in Israel. After the Levite's concubine is outraged, Israel assembles as one man, fights Benjamin at great cost, defeats it by ambush, and burns its cities. They then weep at Bethel at the loss of a tribe, build an altar, devise ways to give Benjamin wives without breaking their oath, and each man goes home to his own tribe and inheritance.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

14 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 1

The children of Israel ask the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites after Joshua's death. When Israel grows strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor rather than utterly driving them out.

Chapter 2

Israel weeps and sacrifices at Bochim after the angel's rebuke, then goes out to possess its inheritances and serves the LORD through Joshua's days and those of the elders. Afterward Israel does evil, serves the Baals, Baal and the Ashtaroth, and is handed over to plunderers and enemies. It is distressed, is saved by judges, and keeps relapsing and acting more corruptly than its fathers.

Chapter 3

Israel lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, intermarried with them, forgot the LORD, and served the Baals and the Asheroth. They served Cushan Rishathaim eight years and Eglon eighteen years, and each time cried to the LORD and was saved. The land had rest forty years after Othniel and eighty years after Moab was subdued.

Chapter 4

The children of Israel again did evil after Ehud died, were sold to Jabin, and were oppressed mightily for twenty years, crying out to the LORD. They came to Deborah for judgment. After the victory over Sisera, their hand prevailed more and more until they destroyed Jabin.

Chapter 5

Israel is remembered as having had unoccupied highways and no ruler until Deborah arose, after choosing new gods and having no shield or spear among forty thousand. Some tribes came to fight while others stayed away, and after the victory the land had rest forty years.

Chapter 6

Israel did evil in the LORD's sight and was brought very low under Midian, hiding in dens, caves and strongholds while their harvests and livestock were destroyed. They cried to the LORD, were rebuked through a prophet for not listening to him, and were then given Gideon as a deliverer. Parts of Israel, including Abiezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, gathered to follow Gideon.

Chapter 7

Israel is the people for whom the LORD gives victory over Midian, and the LORD wants to prevent it from claiming the victory as its own. Men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh gather and pursue Midian after the army flees.

Chapter 8

The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, with his son and grandson, because he saved them from Midian. They willingly give their plunder's golden earrings, then play the prostitute with the ephod, and after Gideon dies they turn to the Baals, forget the LORD, and show no kindness to Gideon's house.

Chapter 10

Israel was led by Tola for twenty-three years and Jair for twenty-two years, then again did evil and was sold to the Philistines and Ammonites. It cried out, confessed its sin, put away the foreign gods and served the LORD. It then assembled at Mizpah against the Ammonites.

Chapter 11

Israel is attacked by the children of Ammon and defended by Jephthah's account of its history: refused passage by Edom and Moab, it went around them, and after Sihon the Amorite fought it, the LORD gave it his land. Israel is said to have lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and the Arnon cities for three hundred years, and its daughters came to celebrate Jephthah's daughter yearly for four days.

Chapter 13

The children of Israel again did evil in the LORD's sight. As a result, the LORD delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.

Chapter 19

The chapter opens by noting there was no king in Israel. The Levite sends pieces of his concubine's body throughout all of Israel's borders, and everyone who sees them says no such deed has been done since Israel came up out of Egypt, urging that it be considered, counsel taken, and a word spoken.

Chapter 20

The children of Israel assemble as one man at Mizpah, hear the Levite's account, and vow not to go home until they have dealt with Gibeah. After Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men, they lose twenty-two thousand and then eighteen thousand in battle, inquire of the LORD at Bethel with weeping, fasting and offerings, and on the third day use an ambush and a feigned retreat to defeat Benjamin and burn its cities.

Chapter 21

The children of Israel weep at Bethel, build an altar, and offer burnt and peace offerings, grieving that a tribe is lacking. They devise ways to supply Benjamin with wives without breaking their oath, and at the end each man departs to his own tribe, family and inheritance.

Israel in The First Book of Samuel

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people of the LORD, his chosen people, whose story in these records runs from defeat and repentance through the demand for a monarchy to the collapse of Saul's reign. It begins with defeats by the Philistines, about four thousand men lost and then thirty thousand, even after the ark is brought into camp. Israel then laments for twenty years, removes the Baals and Ashtaroth, serves the LORD only, fasts at Mizpah, and confesses sin. It pursues the Philistines, recovers its cities from Ekron to Gath, and has peace with the Amorites. The central turning point is the demand of the elders and people for a king like all the nations. The LORD notes Israel's long history of forsaking him since Egypt, and Samuel charges that the people rejected the LORD as their king. Saul is chosen, and Israel shouts 'Long live the king!', though some worthless fellows despise him. Israel comes out as one man at Bezek, three hundred thousand plus thirty thousand from Judah, wins the victory, and makes Saul king at Gilgal. After thunder and rain the people fear the LORD and confess adding this evil to their sins. They are told to keep following him and are warned that they and their king will be consumed if they keep doing evil. Under Saul, Israel's condition worsens. It is considered an abomination to the Philistines, hides in caves and scatters, and has no blacksmith, relying on the Philistines to sharpen farm tools, so only Saul and Jonathan have a sword or spear. The LORD saves Israel in battle, but the people sin by eating meat with blood and are distressed by Saul's oath. They refuse to let Jonathan die. The LORD rejects Saul and tears the kingdom of Israel from him. Israel flees when Goliath appears, then pursues the Philistines after David kills him, and all Israel loves David. After all Israel mourns Samuel, Saul encamps at Gilboa, and Samuel declares the army will be delivered to the Philistines. In the end the men of Israel flee and fall on Mount Gilboa. Saul and his sons die, and people beyond the valley and the Jordan abandon their cities, which the Philistines occupy.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

13 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 4

Israel was defeated by the Philistines, losing about four thousand men, then brought the ark into camp and shouted greatly. In the second battle Israel was defeated again, thirty thousand footmen fell, and each man fled to his tent.

Chapter 7

Israel laments after the LORD for twenty years, then removes the Baals and Ashtaroth and serves the LORD only. At Mizpah they fast, pour out water, and confess they have sinned, and they ask Samuel not to stop crying to the LORD for them. They pursue and strike the Philistines, recover their cities and border from Ekron to Gath, and have peace with the Amorites.

Chapter 8

Israel is the nation Samuel's sons judged and whose elders and people demand a king to be like all the nations. The LORD notes its history of forsaking him and serving other gods since he brought it out of Egypt. At the end the men of Israel are told to go each to their own city.

Chapter 9

Israel is the people the LORD says he has looked upon because their cry has come to him, and whom the chosen man is to save from the Philistines. Samuel says all Israel desires Saul and his father's house. The text notes that no one among the children of Israel was more handsome than Saul.

Chapter 10

Israel is reminded that God delivered them from Egypt and all oppressing kingdoms, yet they rejected him by asking for a king. They present themselves by tribes and thousands, shout "Long live the king!" at Saul's selection, and return to their houses. Some worthless fellows among them despise Saul and bring no tribute.

Chapter 11

Israel, whose people weep at the news from Jabesh, come out as one man under the dread of the LORD, numbering three hundred thousand plus thirty thousand men of Judah at Bezek. They win the victory and then make Saul king at Gilgal, rejoicing greatly.

Chapter 12

Israel testifies that Samuel has not defrauded or oppressed them or taken anything from anyone's hand. Samuel charges them with having asked for a king when the LORD was their king, and after the thunder and rain they fear the LORD and Samuel, confess adding this evil to their sins, and ask Samuel to pray that they not die. They are told to keep following the LORD and are warned they will be consumed if they keep doing evil.

Chapter 13

Israel was gathered after Saul to Gilgal, having heard it was considered an abomination to the Philistines. Facing the Philistine army, the people hid in caves, thickets, rocks, tombs, and pits, some crossed the Jordan, and others scattered from Saul. They had no blacksmith and relied on the Philistines to sharpen farm tools, so only Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear.

Chapter 14

Israel is saved by the LORD that day as the battle passes over by Beth Aven, and Hebrews with the Philistines and Israelites hiding in Ephraim join the pursuit. The men of Israel are distressed by Saul's oath, and the people then sin by eating meat with blood before Saul corrects it. The people refuse to let Jonathan die.

Chapter 15

Israel is the people on whose behalf the LORD remembers Amalek's opposition during the exodus from Egypt. Saul was anointed king over Israel and made head of its tribes, but the LORD rejects him from being king over Israel. Samuel says the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from Saul and given it to a better neighbor.

Chapter 17

Israel's army under Saul stands on the opposite mountain from the Philistines, and its men flee and are terrified when Goliath appears. After David kills Goliath, the men of Israel and of Judah shout, pursue the fleeing Philistines, and plunder their camp.

Chapter 28

All of Israel is said to have mourned and buried Samuel in Ramah. Saul gathers Israel and encamps at Gilboa against the Philistines, and Samuel declares that the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into the Philistines' hand.

Chapter 31

The men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. Those on the other side of the valley and beyond the Jordan, seeing the flight and the deaths of Saul and his sons, abandoned their cities, which the Philistines then occupied.

Israel in The Second Book of Samuel

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people of the LORD, a nation redeemed from Egypt and established as God's people forever, and also the land or place the LORD promises to appoint for them so they dwell there, no longer moved or afflicted. Across the records it appears mainly as a collective of tribes, their elders and men, whose loyalty to David shifts repeatedly. The account opens with mourning: Israel's people flee battle, many fall, and the lament calls Israel's glory slain and bids the daughters of Israel weep over Saul. All the tribes then come to David at Hebron, call themselves his bone and flesh, make a covenant, and anoint him king. Thirty thousand chosen men and the whole house of Israel celebrate bringing up the ark, and David is appointed prince over Israel. The LORD promises Israel a place, and David's prayer affirms its unique status. Israel's forces defeat the Syrians twice, and kings serving Hadadezer make peace and serve them. Division follows: Absalom steals the hearts of Israel's men, they cross the Jordan with him, and Israel is struck down in the forest of Ephraim, twenty thousand slain, before all flee to their tents. The people then debate bringing David back, and the men of Israel quarrel with Judah, claiming ten parts in the king. Some then follow Sheba, who dies, and the people disperse. The close shows Israel under the LORD's anger, counted from Dan to Beersheba with 800,000 swordsmen, and seventy thousand die in a pestilence that is removed after David's offerings.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

11 sections; each heading opens the text

The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1

Israel's people are reported to have fled the battle, with many fallen and dead. David and his men mourn for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel who fell by the sword, and the lamentation calls Israel's glory slain on its high places and tells the daughters of Israel to weep over Saul.

Chapter 5

All the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron, call themselves his bone and flesh, and recall that he led Israel out and in under Saul. Their elders make a covenant with him and anoint him king over Israel.

Chapter 6

Israel's chosen men, thirty thousand, accompany David, and all the house of Israel plays instruments before the LORD. They bring up the ark with shouting and trumpet sound, and the whole multitude, men and women, each receive a portion of bread, dates, and raisins before departing home. David is described as appointed prince over Israel.

Chapter 7

The LORD says he will appoint a place for his people Israel, plant them there, and keep them from being moved or afflicted by the children of wickedness as before. In his prayer David describes Israel as a unique nation, redeemed from Egypt and from other nations and their gods, and established as God's people forever.

Chapter 10

Israel's forces defeated the Syrians twice, first under Joab and then under David at Helam. After the second victory, the kings serving Hadadezer made peace with Israel and served them.

Chapter 15

The men of Israel had their hearts stolen by Absalom's conduct at the gate. Spies were sent through all the tribes to proclaim Absalom king at the trumpet, and a messenger told David that Israel's hearts were after Absalom.

Chapter 17

The elders of Israel were pleased with Ahithophel's saying, but Absalom and all the men of Israel then judged Hushai's counsel better. Israel crossed the Jordan with Absalom and encamped in the land of Gilead.

Chapter 18

Israel, the side opposing David, was struck down before David's servants in the forest of Ephraim, with twenty thousand men slain. After Joab stopped the pursuit and Absalom was buried under stones, all Israel fled, each man to his own tent.

Chapter 19

Israel's people, who had fled each to his tent, argue among themselves about bringing the king back, and then half of them help bring him over. The men of Israel accuse Judah of stealing the king away, claim ten parts in him and more claim to David, and complain that their advice was not sought first.

Chapter 20

The men of Israel leave David to follow Sheba, while Judah stays with the king from the Jordan to Jerusalem. After Sheba's death, the people disperse, each man to his tent. The chapter closes by listing David's officials over the army, the Cherethites and Pelethites, forced labor, records, and priests.

Chapter 24

Israel is the object of the LORD's anger and is counted from Dan to Beersheba, with 800,000 swordsmen reported, besides 500,000 in Judah. Seventy thousand of its people die in the pestilence, which is removed from Israel after David's offerings.

Israel in The First Book of Kings

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is a people, named from Jacob by the LORD, who is also treated as a land and later a northern kingdom. It begins in prosperity under Solomon: with Judah it is numerous as the sand by the sea, and lives safely from Dan to Beersheba, each man under his vine and fig tree. Its elders and tribes gather to feast and sacrifice before the ark, and Solomon prays for forgiveness when they sin and repent. Warnings follow that abandoning the LORD would cut it off from the land and make it a proverb and byword; it had also been told not to mingle with the nations whose women Solomon loved, and it suffered the adversary Rezon. The pivotal break comes at Shechem, where Israel asks Rehoboam for a lighter yoke, is refused, declares no portion in David, stones Adoram, rebels against David's house, and makes Jeroboam king. They follow his calf worship at Bethel and Dan. A prophecy declares Israel will be struck like a reed, uprooted from the good land, and scattered beyond the River for its Asherah poles and Jeroboam's sins. Kings follow in succession: Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri, Ahab, each following Jeroboam's sin, with war against Judah, attacks by Ben Hadad, and a contested kingship between Tibni and Omri. Under Ahab, the people gather at Mount Carmel, stay silent, then after the fire fall on their faces and declare the LORD is God; Elijah's twelve stones recall the tribes of Jacob. Mustered at seven thousand, Israel defeats the Syrians at Samaria and Aphek despite looking like two little flocks of goats. The record ends with Ahab's war for Ramoth Gilead, Micaiah's vision of Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, the army dispersing after Ahab's death, and Ahaziah beginning to reign in Samaria.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

11 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 4

Israel, together with Judah, is described as numerous as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking, and making merry. The people live safely, each man under his vine and fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba all the days of Solomon. The land is divided among twelve officers who provision the king.

Chapter 8

Israel's elders, tribal heads, and all the men assemble at the feast and sacrifice countless sheep and cattle before the ark. Solomon's prayer asks the LORD to forgive them when they sin and repent, and he exhorts them to keep the LORD's commandments. They keep the feast for fourteen days and go home joyful and glad.

Chapter 9

Israel is warned that if the king or his children abandon the LORD, it will be cut off from the land and become a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Israelites are not made bondservants by Solomon but serve as men of war, servants, princes, captains and chariot and cavalry commanders.

Chapter 11

Israel had been told by the LORD not to mingle with the nations whose women Solomon loved. It suffered the adversary Rezon, who abhorred it, and is the people over whom Jeroboam is promised kingship through ten tribes.

Chapter 12

Israel assembled at Shechem to make Rehoboam king but asked for a lighter yoke, and when refused, declared they had no portion in David and departed to their tents. They stoned Adoram to death, rebelled against David's house, and made Jeroboam king. They then followed Jeroboam's calf worship at Bethel and Dan.

Chapter 14

Israel is told it will be struck like a reed shaken in the water, rooted up from the good land given to its fathers, and scattered beyond the River because of its Asherah poles and the sins of Jeroboam. All Israel mourns and buries Abijah. A new king is foretold to rise over it.

Chapter 15

Israel was ruled by Jeroboam, then Nadab, then Baasha, who reigned from Tirzah. It was at war with Judah, and its northern cities and the land of Naphtali were struck by Ben Hadad. Both Nadab and Baasha did evil, following Jeroboam's sin with which he made Israel sin.

Chapter 16

Israel is led into sin by Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri and Ahab, who follow Jeroboam's way. It sees three changes of king in quick succession, the army proclaims Omri king in the camp at Gibbethon, and the people are then divided between Tibni and Omri until Omri prevails.

Chapter 18

Israel is accused by Ahab of being troubled by Elijah, while Elijah says Ahab has troubled it. All the people are gathered to Mount Carmel, stay silent when asked how long they will waver, and agree to the fire test. After seeing the fire they fall on their faces and declare that the LORD is God. Elijah's twelve stones represent the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the name Israel was given.

Chapter 20

Israel, led by Ahab, is mustered at seven thousand and defeats the Syrians at Samaria, striking horses and chariots. At Aphek it camps like two little flocks of young goats against a Syrian army that fills the country, yet wins a great victory.

Chapter 22

Israel is ruled by Ahab, who goes to war with Syria for Ramoth Gilead after three years of peace. Micaiah sees all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. After Ahab's death the army disperses to their cities, and Ahaziah begins to reign in Samaria.

Israel in The Second Book of Kings

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is both a people and a kingdom/land, with Samaria as its capital where kings reigned and an Asherah remained. It is portrayed as the people the LORD brought out of Egypt and for whom he cast out nations, yet it was torn from David's house and repeatedly sinned. Early on it appears as a land of witness: a captive Israelite girl, the prophet Elisha, and Naaman's conclusion that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Under Jehoram it marched with Judah and Edom against Moab, devastating the land before returning home. Syria attacked it, though Elisha's warnings protected it, and Samaria later endured siege and severe famine. Jehu purged Baal worship, but Israel kept the sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and the LORD began cutting away its territory as Hazael struck east of the Jordan. Under Hazael and Benhadad it was oppressed, left to Jehoahaz with only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, yet was given a savior because of the LORD's covenant. Jehoash recovered cities and defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh, plundering Jerusalem; under Jeroboam the LORD saw its bitter affliction with no helper and saved it rather than blot out its name, restoring borders. Decline followed: rapid succession of kings, Menahem's tribute to Assyria, and Tiglath Pileser's capture of northern lands. Ultimately Israel was carried to Assyria, settled in Halah, on the Habor and in the Medes' cities, because it feared other gods, worshiped Baal and the sky's army, built high places, made calves and an Asherah, passed children through fire, and ignored every prophet. The LORD removed it from his sight, leaving only Judah, and Ahab is later cited as a model of idolatry.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

9 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 3

Israel under Jehoram mustered for war against rebellious Moab and marched with Judah and Edom. After the water appeared, the Israelites struck the Moabites, destroyed cities, ruined land, stopped springs, felled trees, and besieged Kir Hareseth. Great wrath came against them after Mesha's sacrifice, and they returned to their own land.

Chapter 5

Israel is the land from which the Syrians took the little girl captive and where a prophet is said to be able to heal Naaman. Elisha says the healing will show that there is a prophet in Israel, and Naaman concludes that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.

Chapter 6

Israel is attacked by Syria and is protected through Elisha's warnings. Its land is spared further Syrian raids after the Syrians are fed, but later Samaria is besieged and suffers severe famine.

Chapter 10

Israel is purged of Baal worship under Jehu but continues in the sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The LORD begins to cut away its territory as Hazael strikes from the Jordan eastward across Gilead and Bashan.

Chapter 13

Israel was oppressed by Syria under Hazael and Benhadad because of its sins, but was given a savior and lived in its tents as before. It did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, and the Asherah remained in Samaria. The LORD favored it because of his covenant, and Jehoash recovered its cities from Benhadad.

Chapter 14

Israel under Jehoash defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh and plundered Jerusalem. Under Jeroboam, the LORD saw Israel's bitter affliction and saved it by his hand rather than blotting out its name, and its borders were restored.

Chapter 15

Israel saw a rapid succession of kings: Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, and Pekah, with Hoshea killing Pekah and taking the throne. Menahem exacted fifty shekels of silver from each wealthy man in Israel to pay Assyria. Tiglath Pileser took northern lands of Israel and carried their people captive to Assyria.

Chapter 17

Israel is carried away to Assyria and settled in Halah, on the Habor, and in the cities of the Medes because it sinned against the LORD. It feared other gods, followed the nations' practices, built high places, made two calves, an Asherah, and served Baal, passed children through fire, and walked in the sins of Jeroboam. It ignored every prophet's warning, and the LORD removed it from his sight, leaving only Judah.

Chapter 21

Israel is referred to as the people whom the LORD brought out of Egypt and for whom he cast out the nations from the land. The LORD had promised David and Solomon that he would not make Israel's feet wander from the land if they kept his law, and says that the people have provoked him since leaving Egypt. Ahab, king of Israel, is cited as a model for Manasseh's idolatry.

Israel in 1 Chronicles

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people and kingdom of the LORD, described as the offspring of his servant and the children of Jacob, a chosen people made his own forever and redeemed from Egypt. The records present it as a collective that acts largely as a unified body, 'all Israel', whose fortunes are tied to its kings and to its obedience. It is listed by genealogies in the book of the kings of Israel and was the first to resettle its possessions and cities, alongside the priests, Levites and temple servants, while Judah was carried captive to Babylon for disobedience. The account begins with defeat: Israel's men flee the Philistines and fall on Mount Gilboa after Saul and his sons die, and the Israelites abandon their cities to the Philistines. It then turns to unity under David. All Israel gathers at Hebron, calls itself his bone and flesh, and its elders anoint him king according to the LORD's word. Tribes send armed men, Issachar's leaders understand the times, and neighbors bring food amid joy. The assembly agrees to David's plan, and he gathers Israel from the Shihor River of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, the extent of its bounds. Together they bring the ark to Jerusalem with shouting and music. The LORD establishes David's kingdom, exalted for Israel's sake. Israel's song calls it to remember the covenant and the promised land, and the LORD pledges to appoint it a place, plant it, and no longer let the children of wickedness waste it. Under David, Israel's army led by Joab and Abishai routs the Syrians and Ammonites, and the Syrians make peace and serve David. A shadow falls with the census: Israel counts 1,100,000 swordsmen, Judah 470,000, and God strikes Israel so that seventy thousand die; wrath is also tied to Joab's unfinished census, though the LORD had promised to increase Israel like the stars. The records close with transition and hope. The altar stands for Israel, Solomon's throne is promised forever, and the LORD grants peace and quietness and a land subdued before him. Israel is organized into monthly divisions of twenty-four thousand under tribal rulers. Its leaders are urged to keep all the LORD's commandments so they may possess the good land and leave it to their children forever.

14 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 9

All Israel was listed by genealogies written in the book of the kings of Israel. The first inhabitants in their own possessions and cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants, while Judah had been carried captive to Babylon for disobedience.

Chapter 10

The men of Israel flee before the Philistines and fall slain on Mount Gilboa. After seeing that Saul and his sons are dead, the Israelites in the valley abandon their cities and flee, and the Philistines move into them.

Chapter 11

All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, calling themselves his bone and flesh and recalling that he led them out and in even under Saul. Its elders anoint him king, and Israel goes with him to Jerusalem. The mighty men helped make him king together with all Israel according to the LORD's word concerning Israel.

Chapter 12

All Israel's tribes sent armed men to Hebron to make David king, and the rest of Israel was also of one heart. Issachar's leaders understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Neighbors from Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali brought abundant food, for there was joy in Israel.

Chapter 13

All the assembly of Israel agreed to David's plan because it seemed right to all the people. David assembled all Israel from the Shihor River of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, and they went up with him and played before God with songs and instruments.

Chapter 14

Israel is the kingdom over which the LORD has established David, whose kingdom is highly exalted for his people Israel's sake. The Philistines go up to seek David after he is anointed king over all Israel.

Chapter 15

All Israel was assembled at Jerusalem by David to bring up the ark. Together with the elders and captains over thousands, they brought the ark up with joy, shouting, and the sound of cornet, trumpets, cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps.

Chapter 16

Israel, described as the offspring of his servant and children of Jacob, receives food from David and is addressed in the song as the LORD's chosen ones who should remember his covenant and the land promised to them. The people say "Amen," praise the LORD, and then depart each to his house.

Chapter 17

Israel is described as the people the LORD commanded judges to shepherd and whom he will appoint a place, plant, and no longer let the children of wickedness waste. David says no nation is like Israel, whom God redeemed from Egypt, driving out nations before them, and made his own people forever.

Chapter 19

Israel's army, led by Joab and Abishai, put both the Syrians and the Ammonites to flight. When the Syrians regathered, all Israel under David crossed the Jordan and defeated them. As a result the Syrians made peace with David and served him.

Chapter 21

Israel is counted at 1,100,000 men who draw a sword, with Judah counted at 470,000. Because of the census God strikes Israel, and seventy thousand of its men fall in the pestilence.

Chapter 22

Israel is the people for whom the altar of burnt offering stands and over whom Solomon's throne will be established forever. The LORD promises peace and quietness to Israel in Solomon's days. Its princes are commanded to help Solomon, and its land is described as subdued before the LORD and his people.

Chapter 27

Israel is organized into divisions of twenty-four thousand serving the king monthly, with rulers over its tribes. Wrath came on Israel because of Joab's unfinished census, and the LORD had said he would increase Israel like the stars of the sky.

Chapter 28

Israel is the kingdom over which the LORD chose David, and then Solomon, to rule. Its assembled leaders are urged in the sight of all Israel to observe and seek out all the LORD's commandments so that they may possess the good land and leave it as an inheritance to their children forever.

Israel in The Second Book of Chronicles

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is both a people and the land or kingdom they occupy, as presented in 2 Chronicles. It is the people the LORD brought out of Egypt, in covenant with him (the covenant stored in the ark), and given a land said to stretch from Hamath or Dan in the north to the brook of Egypt or Beersheba in the south. Solomon calls it a great people, countless as the dust. Early on, the whole assembly gathers at Jerusalem, sacrifices in vast numbers before the ark, and watches fire come down at the temple dedication. Solomon prays that the LORD would hear and forgive them after defeat, drought, famine, plague or captivity, and return them to their land if they repent. The LORD warns that if they forsake him he will pluck them from the land he gave. The pivotal break comes at Shechem: when Rehoboam refuses to lighten the yoke, Israel declares no portion in David, stones Hadoram, and rebels against David's house, a rebellion that continues to this day. Rehoboam is forbidden to fight them, since the LORD calls them brothers of Judah, and faithful priests, Levites and others leave for Judah. Under Jeroboam the northern kingdom keeps golden calves worshipped as gods and a priesthood of its own making, not of Aaron's line, and drives out the LORD's priests. Abijah's Judah defeats it, with 500,000 chosen men falling. Later records show a mixed relationship: hired Israelite troops are sent home and raid Judah's cities; Joash of Israel defeats Judah, breaks Jerusalem's wall and takes plunder and hostages to Samaria; Israel strikes Ahaz and takes 200,000 captives, but after Oded's rebuke its armed men release them. Many people come over to Asa when they see the LORD with him, though the high places remain. Hezekiah's invitation from Beersheba to Dan to keep the Passover is mocked by many in Ephraim and Manasseh, yet some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come. The account ends with Israelites present destroying pillars, Asherah poles, high places and altars across Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh, then giving tithes and first fruits abundantly, a partial return to the LORD.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

12 sections; each heading opens the text

The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1

Solomon speaks to all Israel, including captains, judges, princes, and heads of the fathers' households, and reigns over Israel after returning from Gibeon. Solomon describes Israel as a great people, like the dust of the earth in multitude.

Chapter 5

The elders of Israel, the tribal heads, and the princes of the fathers' households assembled at Jerusalem, and all the men of Israel gathered to the king at the feast in the seventh month. The congregation sacrificed countless sheep and cattle before the ark.

Chapter 6

The assembly of Israel stands while Solomon blesses them and prays before them. Solomon asks the LORD to hear and forgive Israel when they pray toward the house, whether after defeat, drought, famine, plague, battle or captivity. He also asks that the LORD bring them back to their land when they repent, and that they fear him and walk in his ways.

Chapter 7

All the children of Israel watch the fire come down, bow with their faces to the ground, worship, and give thanks that the LORD is good and his loving kindness endures forever. They offer sacrifices, keep the feast from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, and are sent home joyful on the twenty-third day of the seventh month. The LORD warns that if they forsake him, he will pluck them up from the land he gave them.

Chapter 10

All Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king and petitions him to lighten the yoke in return for service. When the king refuses to listen, they declare they have no portion in David and depart to their tents. They stone Hadoram to death and rebel against David's house.

Chapter 11

Israel is the kingdom Rehoboam intends to fight and bring back under his rule, but the LORD forbids the attack, calling Israel the brothers of Judah. Priests, Levites and those from its tribes who seek the LORD leave to go to Judah and Jerusalem.

Chapter 13

Israel, led by Jeroboam, was accused by Abijah of keeping golden calves and driving out the LORD's priests and Levites. The children of Israel fled before Judah, 500,000 chosen men fell slain, and they were brought under at that time.

Chapter 15

Azariah recalled that Israel had long been without the true God, a teaching priest, and law, but was found by God when it turned to him in distress. Many people came out of Israel to Asa when they saw the LORD was with him, though the high places were not taken away out of Israel.

Chapter 25

Israel supplied 100,000 mighty men hired by Amaziah for one hundred talents of silver, but they were sent home on a man of God's warning. In anger they raided Judah's cities. King Joash of Israel later defeated Judah, broke Jerusalem's wall, and took plunder and hostages to Samaria.

Chapter 28

Israel, as the northern kingdom, struck Ahaz with great slaughter and carried 200,000 women, sons, and daughters captive to Samaria with much plunder. After Oded's rebuke and the Ephraimite leaders' warning that its guilt was already great, its armed men released the captives and the plunder. Ahaz is also said to have walked in the ways of the kings of Israel.

Chapter 30

Israel was invited from Beersheba to Dan to return to the LORD and keep the Passover, with the warning not to be like their fathers who were given up to desolation. Many in Ephraim and Manasseh mocked the couriers, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came, and people from Israel took part in the rejoicing.

Chapter 31

All Israel who were present went out to Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh and destroyed the idolatrous objects, then returned to their possessions and cities. The children of Israel gave first fruits and tithes in abundance in response to Hezekiah's command.

Israel in The Book of Ezra

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the covenant people, called the children of Israel, whose story here moves from restoration to failure and repentance. They gather as one at Jerusalem in the seventh month, keep the feast of booths, and shout praise when the temple foundation is laid. They later dedicate the house with joy and large offerings, and keep the Passover with others who separated from the nations' filthiness. Some, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants, go up with Ezra under Artaxerxes' decree. Ezra then learns that the people, priests and Levites have not separated from the peoples of the lands and have taken their daughters as wives. His prayer calls them a guilty remnant, once delivered to kings, sword, captivity and plunder, yet revived and allowed to rebuild. Their guilt is increased by foreign marriages. All Israel swears to follow Ezra's plan, a great assembly weeps bitterly, and many families are listed as having taken foreign wives.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 3

The children of Israel, living in their cities, gathered as one man to Jerusalem in the seventh month. They offered the burnt offerings and kept the feast of booths, and the people shouted with a great shout of praise when the foundation was laid.

Chapter 6

The children of Israel, with the priests, Levites and the rest of the captivity, dedicate the house with joy and offer one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs and twelve male goats as a sin offering. Those who had returned, together with others who separated from the nations' filthiness to seek the LORD, keep the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread.

Chapter 7

Some of the children of Israel, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, went up to Jerusalem with Ezra. Artaxerxes' decree allowed any of the people of Israel in his realm to go willingly. Ezra had set his heart to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel, and he gathered chief men out of Israel to go up with him.

Chapter 9

The people of Israel, along with the priests and Levites, are reported to have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands and to have taken their daughters as wives. Israel in The Book of Nehemiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the covenant people whose story is traced from exile to renewed commitment. Carried away by Nebuchadnezzar, the returnees go back to Judah and Jerusalem, each to his own city, totaling 42,360 plus 7,337 servants and 245 singers, and they settle in their cities. A retrospective recalls how the fathers, rescued from Egypt and sustained in the wilderness, hardened their necks, made a molded calf, killed prophets, and ignored the commandments, yet the LORD did not forsake them. The people then swear an oath, with chiefs sealing it, to keep marriage restrictions, the Sabbath and seventh year, offerings, first fruits, and tithes, and not to forsake God's house. Finally, on hearing the law, Israel separates the mixed multitude from itself, and Nehemiah warns against profaning the Sabbath, recalling how Solomon was led to sin by foreign women.

Chapter 7

The assembly totals forty-two thousand three hundred sixty, plus male and female servants, singers, horses, mules, camels, and donkeys, and they settle in their cities by the seventh month.

Chapter 9

The fathers saw affliction in Egypt, were rescued through the sea, led by cloud and fire, and sustained in the wilderness. They behaved proudly, hardened their necks, made a molded calf, killed prophets, and ignored the commandments, so they were given into the hands of adversaries. Yet the LORD did not make a full end of them or forsake them.

Chapter 10

The chiefs of the people are listed by name as sealers, and the rest of the people, with wives, sons, and daughters, who had knowledge and understanding, joined in the oath. They commit to marriage restrictions, Sabbath and seventh-year observance, a yearly third-shekel charge, wood offerings by lot, and bringing first fruits, firstborn, and tithes. They declare they will not forsake the house of their God.

Chapter 13

Upon hearing the law, Israel separated all the mixed multitude from itself, in line with the rule excluding Ammonites and Moabites. Nehemiah warned that profaning the Sabbath would bring more wrath on Israel, and recalled that Solomon, king over all Israel, was caused to sin by foreign women.

children of Israel in Judith

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where children of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The children of Israel are a people of Judea, dwelling in the hill country and in Bethulia, who worship the God of heaven and hold Jerusalem and the holy house at the top of Zion as their sanctuary and possession. Achior describes them as descended from the Chaldeans, who left their fathers' gods, sojourned in Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt, were enslaved and freed, took the hill country, were later taken captive for leaving God's way, and have now returned to their God and settled Jerusalem. Their central safeguard is stated by Judith: they will not be punished or defeated unless they sin against their God. The story begins with fear at Holofernes' approach. Obeying Joakim's command, they occupy the mountain tops, shut the passages, fortify villages and hilltops, store supplies and set up barricades, while humbling themselves in sackcloth, ashes and fasting, crying to God not to give their families and sanctuary to the nations. Holofernes' men dismiss them as powerless. At Bethulia they receive Achior, worship God, and pray for pity. Terrified by the enemy multitude, they keep watch and cry to the Lord; besieged and weakened by thirst, they turn on their rulers and demand surrender, but agree to wait five more days. Their elders pray that Judith's purposes bring glory to Israel and exaltation to Jerusalem. The Assyrians marvel that Israel has such women, and Judith's words to Holofernes affirm that the sword prevails only if they sin. The turning point comes with the Assyrians in flight: every Israelite warrior rushes out, pursues them past Damascus and strikes them to Chobai, then returns to take spoils. They follow Judith in armor and garlands, singing, worship and sacrifice in Jerusalem, feast three months, and return to their inheritances. The house of Israel mourns Judith seven days, and in her days and long after no one makes them afraid.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 4

The children of Israel in Judea fear Holofernes' approach, occupy the mountain tops, fortify villages, store supplies, and obey Joakim's command. They humble themselves in sackcloth, ashes, and fasting for many days, crying to God with one consent not to let their families and sanctuary be given to the nations.

Chapter 5

The children of Israel are reported to have shut up the passages of the hill country, fortified the high hilltops, and set up barricades in the plains. Achior describes them as descended from the Chaldeans, having left their fathers' gods to worship the God of heaven, and having sojourned in Mesopotamia, Canaan, and Egypt. They were enslaved in Egypt, freed, and took the hill country, were later taken captive for leaving God's way, and have now returned and settled Jerusalem. Holofernes' men dismiss them as having no power or might.

Chapter 6

The children of Israel descend from Bethulia, untie Achior, lead him into the city, and present him to their rulers. After hearing Holofernes' threats they fall down, worship God, and pray for pity on their low estate. They comfort and praise Achior and call on God all night.

Chapter 7

The children of Israel are terrified at the sight of the enemy multitude, take up their weapons, light fires on their towers and watch all night. Besieged and without escape, they cry to the Lord their God. As thirst weakens them, the people turn on their rulers, demanding surrender, before agreeing to wait five more days.

Chapter 9

Israel is called the inheritance of God, and its race is said to be protected by the Lord alone. Its holy house, the top of Zion, and the covenant are named as the things the Assyrians threaten. Judith recalls that in the past God's dear children, moved with zeal for him, received the spoils of those who defiled a virgin.

Chapter 10

The elders pray that Judith's purposes will bring glory to the children of Israel and exaltation to Jerusalem. The Assyrians, seeing Judith, marvel at the children of Israel because they have such women among them, and say that if they are let go they could deceive the whole earth.

Chapter 11

Judith says her people will not be punished and the sword will not prevail against them unless they sin against their God. She claims that, with food and water running short, they plan to kill their livestock and eat what is sanctified, and that they will then be delivered to Holofernes to be destroyed. Holofernes says they slighted him and brought their troubles on themselves.

Chapter 14

Israel is the people whose house Achior joins, and Judith says all who inhabit its borders shall pursue and overthrow the fleeing Assyrians. Achior says that those in every nation who hear Judith's name will be troubled. The Assyrians call the Israelites slaves who have dealt treacherously.

Chapter 15

The children of Israel, every warrior among them, rush out upon the fleeing enemy, and when they hear Ozias's message they fall upon them with one accord and strike them to Chobai. They return from the slaughter, take possession of what remains, and take many spoils. At the end they follow Judith in armor and garlands, singing.

Chapter 16

Israel sings loudly along with Judith in praise, and its lowly, oppressed people shouted, trembled, and saw the enemy flee. The people worship and offer sacrifices in Jerusalem, feast for three months, and return to their inheritances. The house of Israel mourns Judith seven days, and no one makes them afraid in her days or long after.

Jews in Esther (Greek)

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Jews first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Jews are a nation scattered among the nations, described by Haman as having laws different from others and disobeying the king's laws. Haman plots their destruction, and the king gives him authority; decrees sent to 127 provinces order their destruction and plunder on a set day in Adar. They respond with crying, lamentation, mourning, sackcloth and ashes, and in Susa assemble and fast three days at Esther's instruction, carried out by Mordecai. All Israel cries out to God, facing death. The reversal comes when a letter calls them sons of the living God who live by just laws, granting them the right to use their own laws, help each other, and defend themselves on the thirteenth of Adar. They gain light, gladness and feasting, and many Gentiles become Jews out of fear. They kill five hundred men in Susa on the first day and three hundred more on the fourteenth, while those elsewhere destroy fifteen thousand, taking no spoil. They rest and celebrate, honor Mordecai, and adopt Purim for all generations, observed on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar with gifts of food to neighbors and portions to the poor.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 3

The Jews are described by Haman as a nation scattered among the nations whose laws differ and who disobey the king's laws. Haman plots to destroy them all under Ahasuerus's rule, and the king gives him authority to do as he will with them. They are targeted by decrees sent to 127 provinces for destruction and plunder on a set day in Adar.

Chapter 4

The Jews in every province where the decree was published respond with crying, lamentation, great mourning, sackcloth and ashes. Those in Susa are told by Esther to assemble and fast three days for her, and Mordecai carries this out. All Israel cries out with all their might, for death is before their eyes.

Chapter 8

The Jews are granted the right to use their own laws, help each other, and defend themselves on the thirteenth day of Adar against those who attack them. They are told to be ready for that day, and the letter calls them sons of the living God who live by just laws. In every city and province they have light, gladness, feasting and mirth, and many Gentiles are circumcised and become Jews for fear of them.

Chapter 9

The Jews killed five hundred men in Susa on the first day and three hundred more on the fourteenth, while those elsewhere in the kingdom destroyed fifteen thousand, taking no spoil. Israel in The First Book of the Maccabees

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people and land whose fortunes are traced through a period of persecution, resistance, and recovery. It begins divided: some embrace Gentile ways, while many suffer the plundered temple, slaughter, captivity, and a decree forbidding its worship and law. Many refuse unclean food and choose death, and exceedingly great wrath falls upon it. Mattathias's company, joined by the Hasidaeans, tears down altars and circumcises boys, and Israel laments his death. Under Judas Maccabaeus, wrath is turned away, nations begin to fear him, and the king orders Israel's strength destroyed. The people resolve to repair their ruins and fight for the holy place. Deliverance at Emmaus leads to thanksgiving and an eight-day yearly feast of the altar's dedication. Israelites in Gilead and Galilee are rescued and brought to Judea, though about two thousand fall at Jamnia through disobedience. Israel mourns Judas and suffers under Bacchides until peace comes and Jonathan begins to judge, later mourned too. Finally Simon makes peace, and Israel rejoices in confirmed liberty.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 1

Israel was divided, as some of its people embraced Gentile ways while many others suffered. It endured great mourning after the temple was plundered, then slaughter, captivity, and a decree forbidding its worship and law. Many consented to Antiochus's worship, but many resolved not to eat unclean things and chose to die, and exceedingly great wrath came upon Israel.

Chapter 2

Many of Israel gather to the king's officers at Modin, and Israel's mighty men, the Hasidaeans, join Mattathias. Mattathias's company pulls down altars and circumcises uncircumcised boys throughout the coasts of Israel, and all Israel makes great lamentation at his death.

Chapter 3

Israel is protected and its wrath turned away through Judas's deeds, and nations around begin to fear him. It is now targeted by the king's order to destroy its strength and give its land to foreigners by lot. Its people respond by resolving to repair the ruins of their people and fight for the holy place.

Chapter 4

Israel receives a great deliverance on the day of Emmaus and gives thanks to heaven. Judas and the congregation of Israel ordain an eight-day yearly feast of dedication of the altar starting on the twenty-fifth of Chislev.

Chapter 5

Israelites in Gilead and Galilee are attacked, killed, captured, and shut up in strongholds, and they appeal to Judas for help. Those rescued are brought to Judea with their families and goods, and they go up to Mount Zion with joy and burnt offerings. About two thousand fall at Jamnia through the disobedience of Joseph and Azarias.

Chapter 9

Israel made great lamentation for Judas and suffered greatly under Bacchides, worse than at any time since the prophets stopped appearing. After the peace with Bacchides the sword ceased from Israel, and Jonathan began to judge the people.

Chapter 14

Israel rejoiced with great joy when Simon made peace in the land. The people credit Simon, his brothers and his father's house with chasing away Israel's enemies and confirming liberty to Israel.

Jews in The First Book of the Maccabees

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Jews first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Jews are a people regarded by the Gentiles as a state without a ruler, yet permitted by Antiochus to coin their own money. Their story centers on shifting alliances with powerful kings and a lasting friendship with Rome. Under Judas they seek Roman friendship to escape Greek bondage, and Rome registers them as allies and pledges defense against Demetrius. They reject Demetrius's offers, remembering his evil, and side with Alexander. Later Demetrius grants exemptions; three thousand Jewish men save him in Antioch, but he breaks faith. After Jonathan's capture they mourn, fearing neighboring Gentiles who seek their destruction. Jonathan's embassies renew ties with Sparta and Rome. Under Simon, Jews garrison key towns and accept him as leader and high priest. Antiochus confirms tax remissions and coinage, and Rome warns kings not to harm them, though Cendebaeus still raids Judea.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 8

The Jews, under Judas, seek Roman friendship because the Greek kingdom keeps Israel in bondage. They are registered as Rome's allies and friends, and Rome pledges to defend them against Demetrius.

Chapter 10

The Jews were offered release from tributes, taxes, and other burdens, plus enrollment of thirty thousand in the king's forces, by Demetrius, but did not accept them, remembering his past evil. They favored Alexander, who first spoke peace to them, and remained his allies.

Chapter 11

The Jews were declared friends of Demetrius, who granted them exemptions. Three thousand Jewish men saved Demetrius in Antioch, killing about 100,000 of its people and winning glory and plunder. Demetrius later broke faith with them.

Chapter 12

The Jews, through Jonathan and their senate, priests and people, sought to renew brotherhood with the Spartans and friendship with Rome, saying they had been helped from heaven against their enemies. After Jonathan's capture they mourned greatly and became very afraid, and the surrounding Gentiles, saying they had no ruler or helper, sought to destroy them utterly.

Chapter 14

The Jews are called kindred by the Spartans and friends, allies and kindred by the Romans. Under Simon, Jews were placed as garrisons in Bethsura, Joppa, Gazara and the citadel at Jerusalem, and the Jews and priests were pleased that Simon be their leader and high priest forever until a faithful prophet arises.

Chapter 15

The Jewish nation is addressed in Antiochus's letter, which confirms their tax remissions and right to coin money. Their ambassadors had renewed friendship with Rome and brought a gold shield, and Rome's letter tells the kings not to harm them. Under Cendebaeus, the people of Judea are later raided, taken captive and killed.

Jews in The Second Book of the Maccabees

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Jews first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Jews appear as a people chosen by the Lord, bound to laws he ordained, who observe the Sabbath and the feast of weeks, yet who are also described as bound by many sins that turned the Lord's eye away. The records trace their fortunes in a time of persecution and recovery. Early on, they feel indignation at the unjust murder of Onias and appeal to the king, while those who adopted Greek ways are punished by the very men they imitated. Jerusalem's Jews then suffer Jason's slaughter, Antiochus's massacre, enslavement and plundering of the temple, and an attack on the Sabbath, which the narrator attributes to their sins and a brief anger of the Lord. Judas Maccabaeus and a small company escape to the mountains. Persecution deepens: they are forced from their fathers' laws, forbidden the Sabbath, feasts and confessing themselves Jews, made to eat sacrifices and join the Dionysus procession, and many are killed, including women who circumcised their children and people burned in caves for secretly keeping the Sabbath. This is framed as chastening, since God does not forsake his people. Those who stay fight under Maccabaeus, keep the Sabbath, share spoils with the vulnerable, and win victories, and Nicanor admits they are invulnerable when they follow their God's laws. Antiochus threatens to make Jerusalem their graveyard, but after affliction vows to make them equal to Athenians. After lament and prayer they rout Lysias's army with divine help and obtain peace, recognition of rights, and restoration of temple and customs through letters. Conflicts continue at Joppa, Jamnia and elsewhere, with fasting and prayer before battle, a betrayer imprisoned, and the king finally swearing to honor their rights. Divisions appear as some Jews side with Nicanor while others pray, and the elder Razis is hunted. Some compelled to follow Nicanor plead for the Sabbath. After victory the people bless the Lord and decree a yearly commemoration on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Mordecai's day, and the city is held by the Hebrews thereafter.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 4

The Jews, along with many of other nations, felt indignation at the unjust murder of Onias, and those in the city appealed to the king against Andronicus, joined by the Greeks. The text says severe calamity overtook those who adopted Greek ways, as the men they imitated became their enemies and punished them. The three men who spoke for the city were condemned, and even some Tyrians provided magnificently for their burial.

Chapter 5

The Jews of Jerusalem suffered Jason's slaughter, then Antiochus's massacre, enslavement and plundering of the temple, and Apollonius's attack on the Sabbath. The narrator attributes their suffering to their sins, which provoked the Lord to a brief anger. Judas Maccabaeus and a small company escaped to the mountains.

Chapter 6

The Jews are compelled to depart from their fathers' laws, forbidden to keep the Sabbath, observe feasts, or confess themselves Jews, and are forced to eat sacrifices and join the Dionysus procession. Many are killed, including women who circumcised their children and people burned in caves for secretly keeping the Sabbath. The narrator says their suffering is chastening, and that God does not withdraw his mercy or forsake his people.

Chapter 8

The Jews are oppressed and threatened with being sold as slaves, and some cowardly ones flee while others sell their goods and pray for those already sold. Those who stay fight under Maccabaeus, win victories, keep the Sabbath and share spoils with the vulnerable. Nicanor finally acknowledges that they are invulnerable because they follow the laws given by their God.

Chapter 9

The Jews are the target of Antiochus's threat to make Jerusalem their common graveyard and to leave them unburied for animals and birds. After his affliction he vows to make them equal to citizens of Athens, and he addresses a letter to them as worthy citizens asking for their goodwill toward him and his son.

Chapter 11

The Jews lamented and prayed, followed Maccabaeus to battle, and routed Lysias's army with divine help. They then obtained peace and recognition of their rights through letters from Lysias, the king, and the Roman ambassadors, which restored their temple and their ancestral customs and pledged no molestation for those returning home by the thirtieth of Xanthicus.

Chapter 12

Jews were drowned by the men of Joppa and threatened at Jamnia, but under Judas they win a series of battles. The Jews of Scythopolis testify to their neighbors' kindness, and the army keeps the Sabbath at Adullam and afterwards learns that its fallen carried forbidden idol tokens.

Chapter 13

The Jews, facing the loss of law, country, and temple, fasted and prayed for three days and then fought under Judas, showing exceeding boldness that gave the king a taste of their courage. Rhodocus from their ranks betrayed secrets to the enemy and was arrested and imprisoned. In the end the king swore to acknowledge all their rights and made peace with them.

Chapter 14

Jews who had driven Judas into exile flock to Nicanor, while the others sprinkle dirt on their heads and pray to God when Nicanor advances. Their priests swear they do not know where Judas is and pray for the temple, and Razis, one of their elders, is hunted down by Nicanor's soldiers.

Chapter 15

Some Jews compelled to follow Nicanor plead with him to honor the Sabbath, saying the living Lord in heaven commanded the seventh day. After the victory the people bless the Lord in their ancestors' language and, in a common decree, ordain that the thirteenth day of Adar be marked with honor, the day before the day of Mordecai. The city is said to have been held by the Hebrews from that time on.

Israel in Psalms

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people of God, identified throughout these records with Jacob, the house of Jacob, and the houses of Aaron and Levi, and spoken of both as a collective and as a single person ("his troubles"). It is God's inheritance, possession, dominion, servant, and a people near to him, whose praises God inhabits. It dwells in Judah and has David as its shepherd. The records open with a hope: Israel will be glad and rejoice when the LORD restores his people's fortunes, and salvation is wished to come out of Zion. The story begins in Egypt. Israel came into Egypt, grew greater than its adversaries, and was hated. God then brought it out with a strong hand, through the Red Sea and the wilderness, and gave it the lands of Sihon, Og, and Canaan under an everlasting covenant, so that it might keep his statutes. Its fathers trusted and were delivered. Israel is repeatedly urged to trust, hope in, and praise the LORD, who is its help and shield. Festival worship is a statute and ordinance for it, and God has shown his word to Israel as to no other nation. The record is not only favorable. Israel repeatedly tested and rebelled against God, with high places and engraved images. It was disobedient and did not listen, so God gave it over to its own stubborn counsels and to the sword. God also testifies against his people in judgment, saying he does not need their offerings, and calls them to thanksgiving and vows. Israel is afflicted from its youth, with its back plowed, yet has not been prevailed against. Enemies rise up, conspire to destroy it as a nation, and covet its pasture lands, but the LORD's help is in his name. The records move toward redemption: God gathers Israel's outcasts, is asked to redeem it from all its troubles, and will redeem it from all its sins. Israel is urged to hope in the LORD from now and forevermore. It ends in praise: God lifts up Israel's horn, and Israel and the children of Zion rejoice in their King with dance, tambourine, and harp.
