God's people (Israel, your sons) in The Wisdom of Solomon

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where God's people (Israel, your sons) first appears

Abstract written by a model

God's people, called his servants, children, and 'your sons', belong to God even when they sin, because they know his dominion and trust him. They are heirs of the Lord's oaths and covenants made with their fathers, and are taught that the righteous must be kind and that God gives sinners repentance. When chastened, they are to ponder his goodness and look for mercy, while their enemies are scourged far more. They were not led astray by idol worship, though oppressed by idol-worshiping enemies. In the wilderness they receive quails and angels' food, are healed by God's word, and are troubled only briefly by beasts and serpents, with a token of salvation recalling the law. They are guided by a pillar of fire, glorified by the same means that punish their enemies, and as holy children secretly offer sacrifice and agree to the covenant of the divine law, sharing good things and perils. They also suffer death in the wilderness, though the wrath is brief.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 12

God's people, called 'your sons', are described as heirs of the Lord's oaths and covenants of good promises to their fathers, and their fathers were the instruments of destroying the land's old inhabitants. The Lord taught them through his dealings that the righteous must be kind, and gave them good hope because he gives repentance to sinners. When chastened, they are to ponder his goodness when they judge and look for mercy when they are judged, while their enemies are scourged ten thousand times more.

Chapter 15

The speakers say they are God's even if they sin, since they know his dominion, and that they will not sin, knowing they have been accounted his. They say they were not led astray by any evil human plan or by painters' labor on colored images. They were oppressed by enemies who worshiped idols.

Chapter 16

God's people are given quails as a delicacy after a short lack, and are troubled only briefly by wild beasts and serpents, with a token of salvation to remind them of the law. They are healed by God's word, fed with angels' food, and taught that God's word, not crops, preserves those who trust him.

Chapter 18

The holy ones had great light, were guided by a pillar of fire, and were glorified by the same means by which their enemies were punished. Their fathers had been forewarned of the night, and the holy children secretly offered sacrifice and agreed to the covenant of the divine law. They also suffered death in the wilderness, though the wrath did not last long.

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people called by the Lord's name, his portion and firstborn-like inheritance, composed of the tribes of Jacob. It is first named as the place of Wisdom's inheritance. A prayer pleads for mercy and for the tribes to be gathered. Moses received the law to teach them, and Aaron and the priesthood blessed and enlightened them, with Phinehas atoning for them. Joshua gave them their inheritance, and only he and Caleb of six hundred thousand entered the promised land. David received a glorious throne in Israel. After Solomon the kingdom divided, Jeroboam led Israel into sin, and its people were removed from their land.

Chapter 36

Israel is the people called by the Lord's name, likened to a firstborn, and the object of a plea for mercy. The prayer asks that all the tribes of Jacob be gathered and taken as his inheritance as from the beginning, and invokes the blessing of Aaron over the people.

Chapter 45

Israel is the people whom Moses was given the law to teach, and whom Aaron was authorized to enlighten in God's law and to bless through the priesthood. The engraved stones on Aaron's garment correspond to the number of Israel's tribes. Phinehas made atonement for Israel, and the chapter closes with a prayer for wisdom to judge God's people in righteousness.

Chapter 46

Israel is the people to whom Joshua gave their inheritance, and he was made great for the saving of God's elect. Of six hundred thousand on foot, only Joshua and Caleb were preserved to bring them into the land flowing with milk and honey. Caleb's example was meant to let all the children of Israel see that it is good to follow the Lord.

Chapter 47

Israel is the people from whom David was separated, and David received a glorious throne in Israel. Its sovereignty was divided after Solomon, and Jeroboam made Israel to sin. Its people were eventually removed from their land.

Jacob in The Book of Isaiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Jacob first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jacob, also called Israel and Jeshurun, is the LORD's chosen people and servant, addressed throughout these records as both a collective nation (the house of Jacob) and, in the final chapter, a figure tied to a servant who speaks. The records open with compassion and restoration: Jacob will be joined by foreigners and returned to his own land. Then comes a darker picture. Jacob's glory will be made thin, leaving only a few gleanings like olives on a shaken tree. He is a plundered people, robbed and captive with no deliverer, and the text says this happened because he sinned, would not walk in the LORD's ways, and disobeyed the law. He complains that his way is hidden from the LORD, yet he is accused of not calling on him, of neglecting offerings, and of wearying him with sins. He is called obstinate, treacherous, and a transgressor from the womb, and is warned he will be made a curse. Alongside this runs a steady current of grace. He was created, redeemed, called by name, and is precious and honored. He was chosen and refined in the furnace of affliction, and the LORD has not forgotten him. His sins are blotted out and his iniquity forgiven, so that idolatrous altars fall. He is promised the outpouring of the Spirit, offspring who take his name, and a future in which he will no longer be ashamed, will take root, blossom, and fill the world with fruit, and his children will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob. He is told to leave Babylon, and it is proclaimed that the LORD has redeemed his servant. The arc ends with the servant's voice: called from the womb, his mouth made like a sharp sword, hidden in the LORD's quiver as a polished shaft. He laments laboring in vain but trusts the LORD for justice. Raising up Jacob is called too light a task, so he is appointed a light to the nations, the LORD's salvation to earth's end, and a covenant for the people. Though despised by man and abhorred by the nation, kings will rise and worship. Overall the records move from promise, through judgment and rebuke, to redemption and a widening, universal purpose.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 14

Jacob is the object of the LORD's compassion, and the house of Jacob will be united with foreigners who join themselves to it. This is part of the promise of restoration to their own land.

Chapter 17

The glory of Jacob will be made thin and the fatness of his flesh will become lean. He is compared to a field after harvest, with only a few gleanings remaining, like two or three olives left on the top bough of a shaken tree.

Chapter 27

In days to come Jacob will take root, and Israel will blossom and bud, filling the surface of the world with fruit. Jacob's iniquity will be forgiven, and the fruit of taking away his sin is that the altar stones become like beaten chalk and the Asherah poles and incense altars rise no more.

Chapter 29

The LORD, who redeemed Abraham, says concerning the house of Jacob that Jacob will no longer be ashamed and his face will not grow pale. When he sees his children, the work of the LORD's hands, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and stand in awe of the God of Israel.

Chapter 40

Jacob, together with Israel, is rebuked for complaining that his way is hidden from the LORD and that the justice due him is disregarded by God. He is reminded that the everlasting Creator neither faints nor tires and that his understanding is unsearchable.

Chapter 42

Jacob, paired with Israel, is described as having been given as plunder to robbers by the LORD. The text says this happened because the people sinned against the LORD, would not walk in his ways, and disobeyed his law.

Chapter 43

Jacob, also called Israel, is told by the LORD not to be afraid, since he is created, redeemed, called by name, and precious and honored in the LORD's sight. He is also accused of not calling on the LORD, of neglecting offerings, and of wearying him with sins, and is finally warned that he will be made a curse.

Chapter 44

Jacob is addressed as the LORD's servant, chosen and formed from the womb, and told not to be afraid. His descendants are promised the outpouring of the Spirit and blessing, and some will take the name of Jacob. He is told to remember that he is the LORD's servant and is redeemed, and the LORD will be glorified in Israel.

Chapter 48

Jacob, also called Israel and the house of Jacob, is accused of swearing by the LORD's name without truth or righteousness and of being obstinate, treacherous, and a transgressor from the womb. The LORD spares and refines him in the furnace of affliction, and says that obedience would have brought peace like a river and offspring like sand. Jacob is called to leave Babylon, and it is proclaimed that the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob.

Chapter 49

The servant says the LORD called him from the womb, made his mouth like a sharp sword, and hid him in his quiver. He laments having labored in vain but trusts the LORD for justice and reward. The LORD tells him that raising up Jacob is too light a task and gives him as a light to the nations and a covenant for the people, though he is despised by man and abhorred by the nation, and kings will rise and worship.

house of Jacob in The Book of Isaiah

Abstract written by a model

The house of Jacob is a people of the LORD, portrayed across three chapters as both cherished and faulted. It is first urged to walk in the LORD's light, yet described as forsaken: practicing divination like the Philistines, clasping hands with foreigners, and filling its land with silver, gold, horses, chariots, and idols made by its own hands. Next, God calls it to listen, reminding it that he has carried it from birth and will carry and deliver it into old age. Finally it is charged with sin despite daily seeking God, rebuked for oppressing laborers while fasting, and offered restoration and the heritage of Jacob.

Chapter 46

The house of Jacob is called by God to listen. It is told that it has been carried by him from birth and from the womb, and that he will carry and deliver it even to old age and gray hairs.

Chapter 58

The house of Jacob is charged with disobedience and sins, even though they seek God daily and delight to know his ways. They complain that their fasts go unnoticed, but are told they oppress laborers and fast for strife. They are offered restoration and called to build old waste places, with the promise of being fed with the heritage of Jacob their father.

children of Israel in The Book of Isaiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where children of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The children of Israel, also called Jacob and Jeshurun, are portrayed as both a people and a servant figure of the LORD. They are offspring of Abraham, chosen and upheld by the LORD, yet deeply revolted against him, making idols of silver and gold with their own hands, and described as blind and deaf, seeing without observing and hearing without listening. Called a worm, they are told not to fear, since the LORD holds their right hand and will make them a new threshing instrument that threshes mountains and hills. The servant has the LORD's Spirit and brings justice faithfully and gently, not breaking a bruised reed; he is a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners. Early passages mention their glory as a comparison for Damascus's remnant and call them to return and cast away their idols. Later they are named the LORD's witnesses that there is no other God, promised they will not be forgotten, their transgressions blotted out like a cloud, and redeemed, so that heaven and earth sing as the LORD glorifies himself in Israel.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 17

The glory of the children of Israel is the standard to which Damascus's remnant is compared in verse 3. Their forsaken places in the woods and on the mountain top are also the comparison for the strong cities that will become a desolation.

Chapter 31

The children of Israel are told to return to the one from whom they have deeply revolted. In that day everyone will cast away the idols of silver and gold their own hands made, which are called sin.

Chapter 41

Israel, called Jacob, the LORD's chosen servant and offspring of Abraham his friend, is told not to fear because the LORD is with them and holds their right hand. Though called a worm, they will be made a new sharp threshing instrument that threshes mountains and hills, and they will rejoice and glory in the Holy One of Israel.

Chapter 42

The servant is upheld and chosen by the LORD, who delights in him and puts his Spirit on him. He will bring justice faithfully and gently, not shouting, not breaking a bruised reed or quenching a dimly burning wick, and he will not fail or be discouraged until justice is set on the earth. He is called to be a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners, though a later passage speaks of the LORD's servant and messenger as blind and deaf, seeing many things without observing and having open ears without listening.

Chapter 44

Israel, also called Jeshurun, is chosen by the LORD and called his witnesses to the fact that there is no other God. The LORD says Israel will not be forgotten, that its transgressions are blotted out like a cloud, and that it is redeemed and should return to him. Heaven and earth are called to sing because the LORD will glorify himself in Israel.

Israel in The Book of Isaiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is presented in these records as a group, a people and nation, whose story moves from rebellion and ruin to restoration. It begins as a rebellious, sinful nation that lacks knowledge of the LORD, unlike the ox and donkey. It is loaded with iniquity, wounded from foot to head, and has forsaken the LORD. Its country is desolate and its cities burned. Only a very small remnant left by the LORD of Armies keeps it from being like Sodom and Gomorrah. As the LORD's vineyard it was expected to yield justice and righteousness but produced oppression and a cry of distress. Judgment follows. The Syrians in front and the Philistines behind devour it, and the LORD cuts off head and tail in one day. Its leaders, the honorable elder and the lying prophet, lead the people astray, and the people have not sought the One who struck them. Although numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return, and that remnant will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth, and need not fear Assyria. The turn comes with promises of the future. The LORD will choose Israel again and set it in its own land. It will rule its oppressors and take captive those who held it captive. It will be third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing within the earth, and the LORD calls it his inheritance. Israel is named his chosen and servant, for whose sake Cyrus is called. It is described as a new sharp threshing instrument made by the LORD. It is saved with an everlasting salvation, and all its offspring will be justified in the LORD. The LORD is its Redeemer and Holy One, who carried it from birth and will grant it his glory. The closing image is a forsaken wife, barren and widowed, called back by the LORD. She is promised restoration, an enlarged dwelling, establishment in righteousness, distance from oppression and terror, and protection from every weapon formed against her as the heritage of the LORD's servants.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1

Israel is portrayed as a rebellious child that does not know or consider its owner, unlike the ox and donkey. It is called a sinful nation loaded with iniquity, wounded from foot to head, with its country desolate and cities burned. Only a very small remnant left by the LORD of Armies keeps it from being like Sodom and Gomorrah.

Chapter 5

The house of Israel is identified as the vineyard of the LORD of Armies. He looked for justice from it but found oppression, and for righteousness but found a cry of distress.

Chapter 9

Israel receives a word sent by the Lord and is devoured by the Syrians in front and the Philistines behind. The LORD cuts off its head and tail in one day, and its people, led astray by their leaders, become fuel for the fire of his wrath, with no one sparing his brother.

Chapter 10

Israel is described as numerous as the sand of the sea, yet only a remnant will return after a destruction determined and overflowing with righteousness. The remnant of Israel and the escaped of the house of Jacob will no longer lean on the one who struck them but on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. The Lord's people in Zion are told not to fear Assyria, since its yoke will be destroyed and its burden removed.

Chapter 14

Israel will be chosen again by the LORD and set in its own land. The house of Israel will possess peoples as servants and handmaids, take captive those who held it captive, and rule over its oppressors. It is told to take up a parable against the king of Babylon.

Chapter 19

Israel is promised that in that day it will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing within the earth. The LORD names Israel 'my inheritance.' The land of Judah is also said to become a terror to Egypt.

Chapter 45

Israel, called the LORD's chosen, and Jacob his servant, are the reason the LORD has called Cyrus by name. The chapter promises that Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation and never be disappointed or confounded. All of Israel's offspring will be justified in the LORD and will rejoice.

Chapter 46

The remnant of the house of Israel is addressed alongside the house of Jacob as those God has carried from birth. God promises to grant his glory to Israel and salvation to Zion.

Chapter 49

Israel is named as the LORD's servant in whom he will be glorified, and the LORD speaks of bringing Jacob back to him and gathering Israel. The LORD is called the Redeemer of Israel, and the Holy One of Israel is said to have chosen the servant.

Chapter 54

Israel is addressed under the figure of a barren, desolate, forsaken wife and widow, and the LORD is called the Holy One of Israel, her Redeemer. Though cast off for a moment, she is promised restoration, an enlarged dwelling, a city adorned with precious stones, freedom from shame, oppression, and terror, and victory over every accusing tongue.

Ephraim in The Book of Isaiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Ephraim first appears

Abstract written by a model

Ephraim is a northern people and territory headed by Samaria, whose own head is Remaliah's son. It breaks from Judah, allies with Syria, and joins a plot to divide Judah. Its inhabitants speak with pride and arrogance, vowing to rebuild grander after ruin, and it turns on Manasseh while both oppose Judah. The LORD prophesies it will be broken in pieces within sixty-five years, no longer a people. Its fortress will cease alongside Damascus and Syria's remnant. Its drunkards, wearing a proud crown, face woe, and a mighty one sent by the Lord will trample that crown. Yet one passage foresees envy ending and Ephraim reconciled with Judah, acting together against neighboring peoples.

Chapter 7

Ephraim was reported to be allied with Syria and joined the plot to divide Judah. The LORD said that within sixty-five years Ephraim would be broken in pieces so that it would no longer be a people, and that its head is Samaria, whose head is Remaliah's son.

Chapter 9

Ephraim, along with the inhabitants of Samaria, speaks in pride, vowing to rebuild with cut stone and cedars after the bricks and sycamore fig trees fall. It is later described as eating Manasseh while Manasseh eats Ephraim, and together they are against Judah.

Chapter 11

Ephraim's envy will depart, and Ephraim will not envy Judah. The text presents the two as reconciled and acting together against the Philistines, the children of the east, Edom, Moab and Ammon.

Chapter 17

Ephraim's fortress is said to cease, along with the kingdom of Damascus and the remnant of Syria. This places Ephraim in the same coming judgment as Damascus.

Chapter 28

The drunkards of Ephraim are the object of a woe, their crown of pride and fading flower of glorious beauty on the fertile valley being doomed. A mighty one sent by the Lord will cast them down and trample the crown, and it will be like a first-ripe fig eaten as soon as it is seen.

Israel in The Book of Jeremiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the LORD's covenant people, also called Jacob, Ephraim, and the virgin of Israel, and sister to Judah. The records portray it as originally holy to the LORD, his first fruits and firstborn, following him as a bride in the wilderness and held in his hand like clay in a potter's hand. What matters most is the tension between its persistent unfaithfulness and the LORD's refusal to abandon it. Israel forsakes the LORD, digs broken cisterns, and seeks help from Egypt and Assyria. It worships idols and Baal, and its priests, prophets, rulers and fathers all turn away. It is called backsliding, treacherous, uncircumcised in heart, and evil from youth, though it is judged more righteous than treacherous Judah. The account unfolds in stages. First comes remembrance of its early devotion and its subsequent defilement of the land, with a denial of guilt and a warning of shame. Next, the LORD puts it away with a certificate of divorce for its harlotry, yet calls it to return, and its children weep and confess on the bare heights. Judgment follows: lions lay the land waste, Israel is scattered as by an east wind, and it becomes a lost, hunted sheep devoured by Assyria's king and broken by Nebuchadnezzar. It is held captive in Babylon together with Judah, and its wound is called incurable because of its iniquity. Then restoration is promised. The LORD will not forsake it. He is its redeemer, and he will save, heal, multiply and pardon it. He will gather it from the north and all countries, rebuild it, and make an everlasting covenant giving one heart and one way. Ephraim repents and is called a dear son, Rachel's weeping is answered, and the nation will not cease as long as the sun, moon and stars endure. In the days of the righteous Branch it will dwell safely, serving the LORD and David their king, with David's throne never lacking an heir. The final records turn to Babylon, whose slain will fall in return for Israel's slain, and Israel's people are told to flee Babylon and remember the LORD and Jerusalem. The arc runs from holiness through apostasy and exile to promised return and covenant renewal.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

13 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 2

Israel is remembered as holiness to the LORD and first fruits of his increase, who followed him in the wilderness as a bride. Having defiled the land, followed Baal, forsaken the LORD, and sought help from Egypt and Assyria, it has become a captive whose land and cities are laid waste. It denies guilt and is told it will be ashamed and leave with hands on its head.

Chapter 3

Backsliding Israel is said to have played the prostitute on every high mountain and under every green tree and did not return, so the LORD put her away with a certificate of divorce. She is nevertheless called to return and acknowledge her iniquity, and is judged more righteous than treacherous Judah. Her children are portrayed weeping on the bare heights and confessing their sin, shame, and disobedience from their youth.

Chapter 10

The house of Israel is called to hear the LORD's word and is told not to learn the way of the nations or be dismayed at the signs of the sky. Jacob's portion is said to be unlike the idols, since the LORD of Armies, maker of all things, is his name and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance.

Chapter 12

Israel is the people whom the LORD caused to inherit the inheritance that the evil neighbors touch. The house of Judah is to be plucked up from among those neighbors, and the neighbors are told to learn the ways of the LORD's people.

Chapter 16

The children of Israel are recalled as those the LORD brought up out of Egypt. A coming day is promised when he will instead be known as the one who brought them from the land of the north and all countries where he had driven them, and returned them to the land given to their fathers.

Chapter 18

The house of Israel is told by the LORD that it is in his hand as the clay is in the potter's hand. It is also called the virgin of Israel, which has done a very horrible thing, and the LORD says his people have forgotten him, burned incense to false gods, and stumbled from the ancient paths into byways, so that their land will become an astonishment and a perpetual hissing.

Chapter 23

Israel is promised that it will dwell safely in the days of the righteous Branch, and that people will no longer remember the exodus from Egypt but instead the LORD who led the offspring of Israel out of the north country and all countries where he had driven them, so they will dwell in their own land. The prophets of Samaria are said to have prophesied by Baal and caused Israel to err.

Chapter 30

Israel, together with Judah, is promised a return from captivity to the land given to their fathers, where they will possess it. Its wound is called incurable and is attributed to the greatness of its iniquity, yet it is told not to be dismayed, since the LORD will save, heal, multiply, and glorify it. They will serve the LORD and David their king, and will be his people.

Chapter 31

Israel, also called Jacob, Ephraim, and the virgin of Israel, is promised rebuilding, joy, planting of vineyards, and return from the north and distant lands as a great company. Ephraim repents of the reproach of his youth and is called the LORD's firstborn and dear son, and Rachel's weeping for her children is answered with a promise of their return. The LORD says Israel's offspring will not cease being a nation before him as long as the sun, moon, and stars' ordinances continue.

Chapter 32

The LORD says the children of Israel, together with Judah, have done only evil from their youth and provoked him with the work of their hands. Jeremiah recalls how the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders and gave them the land. The LORD promises to gather them from all countries, be their God, give them one heart and one way, and make an everlasting covenant.

Chapter 33

The LORD promises to restore the fortunes of Judah and Israel and build them as at the first, and to perform his good word concerning the house of Israel. Israel is also the throne over which David will never lack a man to sit.

Chapter 50

Israel is portrayed as a hunted and lost sheep, devoured first by the king of Assyria and then with bones broken by Nebuchadnezzar. The LORD promises to bring Israel back to Carmel, Bashan, the hills of Ephraim and Gilead, and to pardon its iniquity so that none is found. Israel will come weeping with Judah to seek the LORD in an everlasting covenant.

Chapter 51

Israel and Judah are said not to be forsaken by their God, though their land is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. Babylon has made Israel's slain fall, so Babylon's slain will fall in return. Zion and Jerusalem cry out for vengeance, and Israel's people are told to flee Babylon and remember the LORD and Jerusalem.

people of Judah and Jerusalem in The Book of Jeremiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where people of Judah and Jerusalem first appears

Abstract written by a model

The people of Judah and Jerusalem are a group called by the LORD's name, yet portrayed as foolish, rebellious, and ignorant of him and his law. They are skilled in evil but not in doing good, given to covetousness from least to greatest, deceitful, perpetually backsliding, and unashamed of abomination. They refuse to hear his words, serve other gods, love to wander, and will not return. The account unfolds across five chapters. First, they are urged to circumcise their hearts and lament, since the LORD's anger has not turned back, and leaders will be astonished. Next, they are charged with backsliding and ignorance of the law, unlike migrating birds; their wives, fields, and harvest will be lost. Then they are likened to a ruined belt and to those who cannot change, like the Ethiopian's skin or the leopard's spots, and are to be scattered like stubble. In the drought they confess their sins and plead for his name's sake, but the LORD does not accept them because of their wandering. Finally, because they rejected him and went backward, they are cast out, winnowed, bereaved, plundered, sent with their enemies to an unknown land, and their remnant given to the sword.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 4

The people are told to circumcise their hearts, flee to fortified cities, and lament in sackcloth, since the LORD's fierce anger has not turned back. The LORD calls them foolish children who do not know him, skillful in evil but not in doing good. At that day the hearts of the king and princes will perish, and priests and prophets will be astonished.

Chapter 8

The people of Jerusalem are charged with perpetual backsliding, clinging to deceit, covetousness, and shamelessness, and with not knowing the LORD's law, unlike the migrating birds that know their times. Their wives and fields will be given to others, their harvest will fail, and they lament that they looked for peace and found dismay.

Chapter 13

This evil people refuse to hear the LORD's words, walk in the stubbornness of their heart, and go after other gods to serve and worship them. They will become like the ruined belt, profitable for nothing. They are likened to those who cannot change, as the Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the leopard his spots, and they are to be scattered like stubble before the wind because they forgot the LORD and trusted in falsehood.

Chapter 14

The people suffer the drought, confess their sins, and plead for the LORD to act for his name's sake and not leave them. The LORD answers that they have loved to wander and not restrained their feet, so he does not accept them. They end by acknowledging their wickedness and their fathers' iniquity, asking him not to break his covenant, and resolving to wait for him.

Chapter 15

The people are cast out of the LORD's sight because they rejected him, went backward, and did not return from their ways. They are winnowed, bereaved of children, have their wealth plundered, are sent with their enemies into an unknown land, and their remnant is delivered to the sword.

speakers (the lamenting community) in The Lamentations of Jeremiah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where speakers (the lamenting community) first appears

Abstract written by a model

The speakers are a lamenting community who confess their sin and describe their ruin. Early on they are mocked, made refuse among the peoples, and admit they have transgressed and rebelled and are unpardoned. They are then called cruel like ostriches, with iniquity greater than Sodom, and famine blackens their skin. The lament deepens into losses: inheritance given to strangers, orphaned children and widowed mothers, water and wood bought at a price, relentless pursuers, rule by servants with no deliverer, and hands given to Egypt and Assyria for bread. Joy has turned to mourning and the crown has fallen. They acknowledge their fathers' iniquities and their own sin, and end by asking the LORD to turn them and renew their days.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 3

The speaker's people make him a derision and a song all day long. He weeps without ceasing over the destruction of the daughter of his people, and the people as a whole confess that they have transgressed and rebelled, that they have been covered with anger, and that they have been made refuse among the peoples, facing terror, the pit, devastation and destruction.

Chapter 4

The daughter of my people is described as having become cruel, like ostriches in the wilderness, and her iniquity is said to be greater than the sin of Sodom. Her destruction is marked by mothers boiling their own children for food.

Chapter 5

The speakers lament that their inheritance and houses have gone to strangers, that they are orphaned, must buy water and wood, are pursued, weary, and ruled by servants, and have given their hands to Egypt and Assyria for bread. They acknowledge that their fathers sinned and that they themselves have sinned, and they plead for the LORD to turn them and renew their days.

Israel is portrayed as the people of God, called by his name, who are stiff-necked and have sinned, disobeying the Lord's voice, sacrificing to demons, and forsaking the fountain of wisdom. As a result they suffer plagues, reproach and a curse for the iniquities of earlier generations. God handed them to a foreign nation, Babylon, whose king they were commanded to serve, and they are scattered in an enemy land, few left among the heathen, with sons and daughters carried away. The account moves from confession in chapter 2, where they plead for deliverance because of God's name rather than their fathers' righteousness, to anguished prayer in chapter 3, where they are exhorted to hear the commandments of life and are told God gave them the way of knowledge. Chapter 4 says they were delivered to adversaries not for destruction but because they provoked God, and urges them to take hold of the law, endure patiently, seek God ten times more, and expect their enemy's fall. It ends in restoration in chapter 5: Israel walks safely in God's glory on level ground, shaded by sweet-smelling trees, led with joy, mercy and righteousness.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 2

Israel, together with its judges, kings, princes, and the men of Israel and Judah, is confessed to have sinned and been ungodly, and now is only a few left among the nations. The people plead for deliverance because they are called by the Lord's name, not because of the righteousness of their fathers and kings. They are recalled as a stiff-necked people who will repent in captivity and be restored, never again to be removed from their land.

Chapter 3

Israel prays in anguish, confessing that it and its fathers sinned and are now scattered in an enemy land, grown old in a strange country, defiled with the dead and counted with those in Hades. It is told it forsook the fountain of wisdom, is exhorted to hear the commandments of life, and is finally said to be the one to whom God gave the way of knowledge.

Chapter 4

Israel, addressed also as Jacob and as God's people, is told to take hold of the law and walk toward its light. They were handed to their adversaries not for destruction but because they provoked God with sacrifices to demons and forgot him. They are urged to suffer patiently, return and seek God ten times more, and expect to see their enemy destroyed.

Chapter 5

Israel is to go safely in the glory of God along a level ground made by the lowering of mountains and hills and the filling of valleys. The woods and every sweet smelling tree have shaded Israel at God's command. God will lead Israel with joy in the light of his glory, with mercy and righteousness.

house of Israel in The Book of Ezekiel

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where house of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The house of Israel is portrayed as a collective people, repeatedly called a nation of rebels and a rebellious house, who have transgressed against the Lord together with their fathers to this day. They are described as impudent, stiff-hearted, obstinate and hard-hearted, with eyes and ears that neither see nor hear, and the LORD says they will not listen to Ezekiel because they will not listen to him. The records open with Ezekiel being sent to them, particularly the captives, whether they hear or refuse, so that they will know a prophet has been among them. The central charges are idolatry and abomination: great abominations in the sanctuary, idols portrayed in a hidden chamber, estrangement from the LORD through idols, not walking in his statutes while following the ordinances of surrounding nations, and filling Jerusalem with the slain. They defiled the land and profaned the holy name among the nations. They quote the sour grapes proverb and accuse the LORD of an unfair way, but he answers that their own way is unfair and that he will judge each according to his ways. They lament that their sins are upon them and that hope is lost. Signs, a riddle and parable are given to them, and they are told of exile, scattering among the nations, and eating unclean bread. Their reliance on Egypt proved a broken reed. The account then turns toward restoration. The LORD calls them to return, cast away transgressions and make a new heart and spirit. He promises to gather them, cleanse them from idols and filthiness, replace the stony heart, put his Spirit in them, and bring them to the land given to their fathers. The dry bones are identified with the whole house, which will become one nation under one king, with no more division into two kingdoms. A horn will sprout for Israel, and a good cedar is promised. They will remember their evil and loathe themselves, no longer defile the holy name, be shown the house and its pattern, and be accepted. The records end with the whole house receiving a city possession, 5,000 by 25,000, beside the holy portion, with land allotted by tribes and atonement made through the prince's offerings.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

15 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 2

The children of Israel are called a nation of rebels who have rebelled against the speaker, as have their fathers, to this very day. They are described as impudent, stiff-hearted, and a rebellious house, and their words and looks are something the son of man must not fear. Whether they hear or refuse, they will know a prophet has been among them.

Chapter 3

The house of Israel is described as obstinate, hard-hearted and rebellious, and the LORD says they will not listen to Ezekiel because they will not listen to him. They are contrasted with peoples of strange speech who would have listened. Ezekiel is sent to them, particularly to the captives, to say "This is what the Lord GOD says," whether they hear or refuse.

Chapter 4

The house of Israel is the audience of the sign, and its iniquity is borne by the man lying on his left side for 390 days, one day for each year of iniquity. The LORD says its children will eat their bread unclean among the nations where He will drive them.

Chapter 8

The house of Israel is said to commit great abominations at the sanctuary, driving the Lord to go far off from it. Its idols are portrayed on the wall of a hidden chamber, and its elders worship in the dark.

Chapter 11

The house of Israel is said to know the thoughts the LORD knows in their minds, and is charged with not walking in His statutes or keeping His ordinances but following the ordinances of surrounding nations. The LORD promises to gather them, give them one heart and a new spirit in place of the stony heart, so they may walk in His statutes and be His people. Those whose hearts follow detestable things will have their way brought on their own heads.

Chapter 12

The house of Israel is described as a rebellious house with eyes and ears that do not see or hear. They ask Ezekiel what he is doing, and are told that the act concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all Israel among whom he is. They will go into exile and be scattered among the nations, and they are quoted as saying the vision is for many days off.

Chapter 14

The house of Israel is described as estranged from the LORD through its idols, and is called to return and turn away from its abominations. The LORD's aim is that they no longer go astray or defile themselves, but be his people with him as their God.

Chapter 17

The house of Israel receives the riddle and parable and is called a rebellious house that does not understand what these things mean. It is told the interpretation, and the passage ends with the promise of a good cedar planted on the mountain of Israel's height.

Chapter 18

The house of Israel is rebuked for using the sour grapes proverb and for saying that the way of the Lord is not equal or fair. The Lord GOD answers that their own ways are unfair, says he will judge each of them according to his ways, and urges them to return, cast away their transgressions, and make a new heart and spirit.

Chapter 29

Israel is said to have been leaned on Egypt, which proved a staff of reed that broke and tore their shoulders and paralyzed their thighs. After Egypt's judgment it will no longer be Israel's confidence or bring iniquity to memory, and the LORD will cause a horn to sprout for Israel.

Chapter 33

The house of Israel laments that their transgressions and sins are on them and asks how they can live. The LORD urges them to turn from their evil ways, asks why they will die, and tells them he will judge each according to his ways. They accuse the LORD's way of being unfair, though it is their own way that is not fair.

Chapter 36

The house of Israel defiled their land by their ways, deeds, bloodshed, and idols, and profaned God's holy name among the nations. God promises to gather them, cleanse them, give them a new heart and spirit, and make them his people again, after which they will remember their evil ways and loathe themselves. He also says he will be inquired of by them and will increase them like a flock.

Chapter 37

The whole house of Israel is identified with the bones and is quoted as saying, 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost. We are completely cut off.' The LORD promises to open their graves, put his Spirit in them, bring them into their own land, make them one nation under one king, cleanse them from idols, and dwell among them forever.

Chapter 43

The house of Israel is told it will no more defile God's holy name, neither the people nor their kings, through prostitution and the kings' dead bodies. They are to put these away and be shown the house so they may be ashamed of their iniquities and measure the pattern. They are to keep and do its ordinances, and they will be accepted when their offerings are made on the altar.

Chapter 45

The whole house of Israel receives the city possession, 5,000 wide and 25,000 long, next to the holy portion. The princes are to give the land to the house according to tribes, and the prince's offerings make atonement for it.

Israel in The Book of Ezekiel

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel, also called the children of Israel and the house of Israel, is both a people and a land belonging to the LORD. The records portray it as a chosen but rebellious covenant people whose story moves from judgment through scattering to restoration. Early on, Israel (with Judah) is judged to have exceedingly great iniquity. It has a lewd heart that departed from God, plays the prostitute after idols, practices child sacrifice to this day, and rebelled in Egypt and the wilderness. It profaned the Sabbaths, was led astray by false prophets proclaiming peace where there was none, and desires to be like the nations. The people say the LORD has forsaken the land. The LORD calls the house of Israel dross, like bronze, tin, iron, and lead left over from silver, to be melted in the furnace of his wrath in Jerusalem. The land is to be desolate. Its dead will lie before its idols, many will fall by sword, famine, and pestilence, and a remnant will be scattered among the nations, as sworn in the wilderness. Its prince is called a deadly wounded wicked one, and the kingdom is to be overturned. The turn comes with the LORD's promise to gather the scattered flock. Neighbors such as Ammon and Edom rejoiced over Israel's desolate inheritance and mocked its mountains, and the LORD will answer on its behalf. Israel will be his instrument of vengeance on Edom. He will free it from scornful neighbors, bring it back from the sword and from many peoples to the mountains of Israel, and give it the land given to Jacob. There the people will dwell securely, building houses and planting vineyards. They will come to know that the LORD is their God and they are his people. The restored Israel dwells in unwalled villages with livestock and goods, which draws Gog's plan to plunder it. Israel instead burns the fallen army's weapons for seven years and buries Gog's multitude for seven months in the valley of Hamon Gog to cleanse the land. Its captivity, which came because of iniquity, is reversed. It receives mercy, forgets its shame, and receives the Lord's Spirit. The records end with order restored. Israel is rebuked for bringing uncircumcised foreigners into the sanctuary and is taught the difference between holy and common. The twelve tribes divide the land by lot, with Joseph receiving two portions, and aliens living among them are treated as native-born and given an inheritance.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

14 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 6

Israel, called the children of Israel and the house of Israel, will see its dead bodies laid before its idols and its cities laid waste. Some will escape as a remnant among the nations, but others will fall by sword, famine, and pestilence, and the land will become desolate and waste.

Chapter 9

The house of Israel, together with Judah, is judged to have exceedingly great iniquity. The narrator fears that the LORD will destroy all the residue of Israel in pouring out his wrath on Jerusalem, and the LORD replies that he will bring their way on their head.

Chapter 13

Israel is the people and house whose prophets have been like foxes in waste places and have led them astray by proclaiming peace where there is none. The LORD says he will deliver his people from the hands of those who ensnare them. He also says the false prophets will not be written in the writing of the house of Israel or enter the land of Israel.

Chapter 20

Israel is shown as a people chosen by the LORD who rebelled in Egypt and the wilderness, profaned his Sabbaths, and continued in idolatry, including child sacrifice, to the present day. The LORD promises to gather them, judge them, purge the rebels, and bring the rest into the land to serve him on his holy mountain, where they will loathe their past evils.

Chapter 21

The land of Israel is told that the LORD is against it and that his sword will cut off the righteous and the wicked from the south to the north. His people and all the princes of Israel are delivered over to the sword. Its prince is called a deadly wounded wicked one whose day has come, and the kingdom is to be overturned until the rightful one comes.

Chapter 22

The house of Israel is called dross to the LORD, like bronze, tin, iron, and lead left over from silver. They will be gathered into Jerusalem and melted by the fire of his wrath, and will know that the LORD has poured out his wrath on them. They are also to be scattered among the nations.

Chapter 25

The land of Israel is said to have been made desolate, and Ammon rejoiced over it with contempt. The LORD says he will lay his vengeance on Edom by the hand of his people Israel, who will act according to his anger and wrath.

Chapter 28

The house of Israel will no longer suffer a pricking brier or hurting thorn from scornful neighbors. The LORD will gather them from the peoples among whom they are scattered and show himself holy among them, and they will dwell securely in their own land given to Jacob, building houses and planting vineyards.

Chapter 34

Israel is the land and people whose shepherds failed them, and whose scattered flock the LORD will bring back to their own land, to the mountains of Israel, to feed on good pasture. The house of Israel will come to know that the LORD their God is with them and that they are his people.

Chapter 35

Israel, called the children of Israel and the house of Israel, was handed over to the power of the sword in the time of its calamity and the iniquity of the end. Its mountains were mocked as desolate and 'given to devour', and its inheritance was rejoiced over. The LORD was there in its land and answers on its behalf.

Chapter 38

Israel is described as a land brought back from the sword and gathered out of many peoples onto its once continually wasted mountains. Its people dwell securely in unwalled villages without bars or gates, with livestock and goods, which draws Gog's plan to plunder them. The LORD calls them his people and his land.

Chapter 39

Israel will burn the weapons of the fallen army as fuel for seven years, plunder those who plundered them, and bury Gog's multitude for seven months to cleanse the land. They will come to know the Lord as their God from that day forward. Their captivity will be reversed, they will receive mercy, forget their shame, dwell securely, and receive the Lord's Spirit.

Chapter 44

The house of Israel is called rebellious and rebuked to stop its abominations, including bringing uncircumcised foreigners into the sanctuary and setting others to perform the duty of the holy things. Its people are to be taught the difference between holy and common and clean and unclean. They are to give the priests offerings, first fruits, and the first of their dough.

Chapter 47

The twelve tribes of Israel are told to divide the land for inheritance by lot, each receiving a portion, with Joseph having two. They are to treat the aliens who live among them and father children there as native-born, giving them an inheritance among the tribes.

Israel in The Book of Hosea

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the LORD's people, addressed throughout the Book of Hosea as a nation, a house, and a son, and it is the subject of an extended indictment followed by a promise of restoration. It is closely tied to Ephraim, which is joined to idols, and is often named alongside Judah. The records open under king Jeroboam son of Joash, with judgment: the land commits great adultery by forsaking the LORD, its kingdom will cease, its bow will be broken in Jezreel, and mercy will end. A future promise is set beside this, that its children will be as countless as the sand of the sea, be called sons of the living God, and be united with Judah under one head. The central charge is unfaithfulness. Israel is stubborn like a heifer, led astray by a spirit of prostitution, and a covenant breaker. It consults a wooden idol, worships at high places under oaks, poplars and terebinths, makes idols of silver and gold, and multiplies altars and sacred stones as its land prospers. It sacrifices to the Baals and burns incense to engraved images. Its pride testifies against it, it is defiled yet not hidden from the LORD, and its heart is divided. It set up kings and princes without the LORD's approval, forgot its Maker while building palaces, and sought Assyria like a wild donkey. It trusts its own way and mighty men and refuses to repent. Its sin is traced back to Gibeah and Baal Peor. The account unfolds from judgment to restoration. The middle chapters show the people refusing to return, being swallowed up among the nations like a worthless thing, losing harvest and land, returning to Egypt, and facing fire on its cities, fallen fortresses, and a king destroyed. The LORD recalls loving Israel as a child called out of Egypt and hesitates to abandon it like Admah and Zeboiim. Chapter 13 says Israel is destroyed because it is against the LORD, its helper. The final chapter calls it to return, gives it words asking forgiveness and renouncing Assyria, horses, and handmade gods, and promises that it will blossom like the lily, root and have fragrance like Lebanon, and have beauty like the olive tree.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

11 sections; each heading opens the text

The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1

Israel, under king Jeroboam son of Joash, is judged: the land commits great adultery by forsaking the LORD, its kingdom will cease, its bow will be broken in the valley of Jezreel, and it will receive no more mercy. Yet its children will become as countless as the sand of the sea, be called sons of the living God, and be gathered with Judah under one head.

Chapter 4

Israel is called to hear the LORD's word and is described as having behaved extremely stubbornly, like a stubborn heifer. It plays the prostitute, and Ephraim is said to be joined to idols. Judah is warned not to follow Israel's offense or go to Gilgal and Beth Aven.

Chapter 5

Israel is not hidden from the LORD and is defiled; its pride testifies to its face. Israel stumbles in its iniquity together with Ephraim and Judah, and the house of Israel is among those addressed in the judgment. Its tribes are told what will surely be.

Chapter 6

Israel is the house in which the LORD says He has seen a horrible thing. It is declared defiled, in connection with the prostitution found in Ephraim.

Chapter 7

Israel is the people the LORD would heal, but the exposure of Ephraim's and Samaria's wickedness prevents it. The pride of Israel testifies to its face, yet they have not returned to the LORD their God or sought him. They are compared to a faulty bow, and their princes will fall by the sword.

Chapter 8

Israel claims to acknowledge God but has cast off what is good, and the enemy will pursue it. It set up kings and princes without the LORD's approval, made idols of silver and gold, and forgot its Maker while building palaces. It is swallowed up among the nations like a worthless thing, will return to Egypt, and will have fire sent on its cities.

Chapter 9

Israel is told not to rejoice like the nations because it was unfaithful to its God and loved a prostitute's wages at every threshing floor. It will lose its harvest and its land and will consider the prophet a fool because of its great sins and hostility. Its fathers were found like grapes in the wilderness but turned to Baal Peor and became abominable like what they loved.

Chapter 10

Israel is portrayed as a luxuriant vine that multiplied altars and adorned sacred stones as its land prospered, yet its heart is divided and it is found guilty. It has sinned since the days of Gibeah, has plowed wickedness and reaped iniquity, and will be ashamed of its own counsel. Its fortresses will be destroyed and its king destroyed at daybreak.

Chapter 11

Israel is remembered as a child whom the LORD loved and called his son out of Egypt, but who sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to engraved images. The people are determined to turn from the LORD, and the house of Israel surrounds him with deceit. The LORD asks how he can give up Israel or make it like Admah and Zeboiim.

Chapter 13

Israel is accused of sinning more and more with idols and of forgetting the LORD after being filled in pasture. The LORD says Israel is destroyed because it is against him, its helper, and asks where its king and judges are to save it.

Chapter 14

Israel is told to return to the LORD because it has fallen through its sin, and is given words to say asking forgiveness and renouncing Assyria, horses, and handmade gods. The LORD promises it restoration: it will blossom like the lily, root like Lebanon, spread branches, and have beauty like the olive tree and fragrance like Lebanon.

Ephraim in The Book of Hosea

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Ephraim first appears

Abstract written by a model

Ephraim is a figurative name for a people, closely tied to Israel, whom the LORD addresses, accuses and judges across these records. The dominant theme is unfaithfulness: Ephraim is joined to idols, likened to a prostitute, defiled, and said to have made molten images from its silver. Its love for the LORD is like a morning cloud or early-vanishing dew, and it has not returned to him despite pride testifying against it. Chapter 5 opens with Ephraim known to the LORD, stumbling in iniquity, oppressed and crushed in judgment. Seeing its sickness, it turns to Assyria, which cannot heal it. Chapter 7 deepens the picture: Ephraim mixes among the nations, is like an unturned pancake and a burning oven, and is a dove easily deceived and without understanding, calling to Egypt and going to Assyria while strangers devour its strength and gray hairs go unnoticed. It is also a faulty bow, returning but not to the Most High. Later chapters turn to coming judgment. Planted like Tyre in a pleasant place, it will nonetheless return to Egypt, be barren, see its children given to the murderer, have its root dried up, and wander among the nations. It is a trained heifer who loves to thresh, and it will receive shame. It feeds on wind, chases the east wind, multiplies lies and desolation, covenants with Assyria, sends oil to Egypt, and boasts of wealth while denying iniquity. It has provoked the LORD bitterly, so its blood stays on it. Once exalted in Israel, it died through Baal, its guilt is stored up, and it is an unwise son who fails to come to the opening of the womb, though fruitful among its brothers. Yet mercy runs alongside judgment. The LORD taught Ephraim to walk and healed it unrecognized, asks how he can give it up, and says he will not execute his fierce anger or destroy it. The story ends with the LORD asking what Ephraim has to do with idols any more, and promising to answer and care for it, with its fruit found in him.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

9 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 5

Ephraim is known to the LORD and accused of playing the prostitute, being defiled, and pursuing idols. It stumbles in iniquity, is oppressed and crushed in judgment, and is to become a desolation. When it saw its sickness it went to Assyria and King Jareb, who cannot heal it, and the LORD will be like a moth and a lion to it.

Chapter 6

Ephraim is addressed by the LORD, who asks what He shall do to it because its love is like a morning cloud and early-vanishing dew. Ephraim is charged with prostitution, and with Israel it is described as defiled.

Chapter 7

Ephraim's iniquity is uncovered, and it is said to mix itself among the nations and to be like a pancake not turned over. Strangers devour its strength and gray hairs appear on it without its noticing, and it is likened to an easily deceived dove without understanding that calls to Egypt and goes to Assyria.

Chapter 9

Ephraim is pictured as planted like Tyre in a pleasant place, yet it will return to Egypt, and its glory will fly away like a bird. Its children will be brought out to the murderer, its root is dried up, and it will bear no fruit. It is struck and cast away, and will wander among the nations because it did not listen to God.

Chapter 10

Ephraim is described as a trained heifer that loves to thresh, and the LORD will put a yoke on her beautiful neck and set a rider on her. Ephraim will receive shame.

Chapter 11

Ephraim was taught to walk by the LORD, who took them by their arms, though they did not know he healed them. The LORD asks how he can give up Ephraim, and declares he will not execute his fierce anger or return to destroy Ephraim. Ephraim is also said to surround the LORD with falsehood.

Chapter 12

Ephraim is said to feed on wind, chase the east wind, and multiply lies and desolation while making a covenant with Assyria and carrying oil into Egypt. He boasts that he has become rich and that no iniquity that is sin will be found in him. He has bitterly provoked anger, so his blood will be left on him and his Lord will repay his contempt.

Chapter 13

Ephraim was once exalted in Israel, but became guilty through Baal and died. His guilt and sin are stored up, he is likened to an unwise son who fails to come to the opening of the womb, and though fruitful among his brothers his spring and fountain will dry up under an east wind, and his storehouse of treasure will be plundered.

Chapter 14

Ephraim is addressed by the LORD, who asks what he has to do any more with idols. The LORD says he answers and will take care of Ephraim, and that Ephraim's fruit is found in him.

Israel in The Book of Amos

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the people of the Lord GOD, called "my people Israel," the children of Israel and the house of Jacob. The records portray a chosen people, brought out of Egypt, led forty years in the wilderness, and given prophets and Nazirites, yet persistently unfaithful. Its transgressions are many: oppressing the poor, selling the righteous and needy for silver and sandals, hoarding plunder in palaces, and lounging on couches and silken cushions in Samaria. It gave Nazirites wine and told prophets not to prophesy. Its worship is hollow: it is sarcastically told to sin at Bethel and Gilgal, boasting of its offerings. Despite hunger, drought, blight, locusts, plague, and the sword, it has not returned to the LORD. The account unfolds from indictment to judgment to partial hope. Early chapters recall the LORD's past acts and announce that Israel will be crushed and punished, with only scraps rescued like a shepherd saving two legs from a lion. It is told to prepare to meet its God. Later a plumb line is set in its midst, its sanctuaries will be laid waste, and captivity is foretold. Amos is sent to prophesy despite Amaziah's opposition. Then comes its declared end: songs become wailing, feasts become mourning, and those swearing by Samaria's sin fall. The final chapter says the sinful kingdom will be destroyed, but the house of Jacob will be sifted among nations without losing a kernel, and promises return from captivity, rebuilt cities, vineyards, gardens, possession of the remnant of Edom, and permanent rooting in its land.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 2

Israel receives the longest indictment and is reminded of the LORD's past acts: destroying the Amorite, bringing them out of Egypt, leading them forty years, and raising up prophets and Nazirites. The people gave the Nazirites wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy, and the LORD will crush them in their place.

Chapter 3

The children of Israel are addressed as the whole family the LORD brought out of Egypt and chose above all earth's families, and are therefore to be punished for their sins. Those who sit at ease in Samaria on couches and silken cushions will be rescued only as a shepherd saves two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth.

Chapter 4

Israel, addressed as the children of Israel, is told sarcastically to go to Bethel and Gilgal and sin, bringing sacrifices, tithes, leavened thanksgiving offerings, and boasted-about free will offerings that please them. It has suffered hunger, drought, blight, locusts, plagues, the sword, and overthrow, yet has not returned to the LORD, and is told to prepare to meet its God.

Chapter 7

Israel is the LORD's people, in the midst of whom he will set a plumb line and not pass by again. Its sanctuaries will be laid waste, and it is said it will surely be led away captive out of its land. Amos is sent to prophesy to Israel, though Amaziah tells him to stop.

Chapter 8

Israel is declared by the Lord GOD to have reached its end, with the LORD no longer passing by them. Its temple songs will become wailing, many dead bodies will be thrown out in silence, and its feasts will turn to mourning like that for an only son. Those who swear by the sin of Samaria, the god of Dan, and the way of Beersheba will fall and never rise again.

Chapter 9

Israel, called the children of Israel and the house of Jacob, is told it is like the Ethiopians to the Lord, who also brought it up from Egypt. The sinful kingdom is to be destroyed from the earth, but the house of Jacob will not be utterly destroyed and will be sifted among the nations without losing the least kernel. Israel is promised a return from captivity, rebuilt cities, vineyards, and gardens, and never again being plucked from the land the Lord gave.

house of Israel in The Book of Amos

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where house of Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

The house of Israel is a collective people, lamented as fallen and called small, whose fate unfolds across three chapters. It is first mourned in a lament, with its cities to be reduced to a tenth of their fighting men. It is accused of trampling the poor, taking bribes, hating the one who reproves in the gate, and turning justice to wormwood. It owns houses of cut stone and vineyards it will not enjoy, and it made idols. It is urged to seek good and establish justice so the LORD may be gracious to the remnant of Joseph. Punishment includes wailing, captivity beyond Damascus, and a nation raised against it. Finally, Jacob, described by Amos as small, pleads, and the LORD relents from the locusts and the fire.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 5

The house of Israel is mourned in a lamentation as fallen, with its cities to be reduced to a tenth of their fighting men. It is accused of trampling the poor, taking bribes, and turning away the needy in the courts, and is told to seek good, hate evil, and establish justice so that the LORD may be gracious to the remnant of Joseph. Its punishment is wailing in the streets and vineyards and captivity beyond Damascus.

Chapter 6

The house of Israel comes to its notable men, who are accused of turning justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness. Addressed directly, it is told that the LORD will raise up a nation against it that will afflict it from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.

Chapter 7

Jacob is described by Amos as small in his pleas, asking how he could stand. Because of these pleas the LORD relents from the locusts and the fire.

Israel in The Book of Micah

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Israel first appears

Abstract written by a model

Israel is the LORD's people, portrayed as a flock and heritage dwelling by themselves in a forest, and as a land. The records show it accused through its rulers of abhorring justice and perverting equity, and of keeping the statutes of Omri and the works of Ahab's house. The LORD contends with it, recalling redemption from Egypt and the Balak and Balaam episode. Judgment comes: it is besieged, its judge struck on the cheek with a rod, its horses, chariots, cities and strongholds cut off, and the land left desolate because of its inhabitants' deeds. Yet restoration is promised. The LORD will gather the remnant like sheep of Bozrah, with the king passing before them and the LORD at their head. They will feed in Bashan and Gilead as of old, have walls rebuilt and boundaries extended, be gathered from Assyria, Egypt and far places, and receive compassion, truth and mercy sworn to their fathers.

Chapter 3

Israel is addressed through the rulers of its house, who are accused of abhorring justice and perverting equity. The speaker is empowered to declare Israel's sin.

Chapter 5

Israel is besieged, and its judge will be struck with a rod on the cheek. The LORD will abandon them until she who is in labor gives birth, after which the rest of the ruler's brothers will return to the children of Israel. The LORD will also cut off its horses, chariots, cities and strongholds.

Chapter 6

Israel is the people with whom the LORD contends and who are told to remember their redemption from Egypt and the episode of Balak and Balaam. Because they keep the statutes of Omri and the works of Ahab's house, they are threatened with ruin and with bearing reproach.

Chapter 7

The LORD's people are called his flock and heritage, dwelling by themselves in a forest, and are asked to be fed in Bashan and Gilead as in days of old. They are promised rebuilt walls, an extended boundary, and a gathering from Assyria, Egypt, and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. Yet the land will be desolate because of its inhabitants' deeds, and the remnant is shown compassion and promised truth and mercy as sworn to their fathers.

the Jews in The Gospel According to John

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where the Jews first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Jews appear in these records as a collective antagonist group whose relationship with Jesus moves from questioning and misunderstanding to hostility and finally to delivering him for execution. They claim descent from Abraham and God as their Father, set their hope on Moses, search the Scriptures believing they hold eternal life, and meet always in the temple. Jesus says they lack God's love, that Moses accuses them, and that their father is the devil. They have agreed to expel from the synagogue anyone confessing Jesus as Christ, and they disbelieve because they are not of his sheep. Their central stance is a persistent desire to kill Jesus. The account begins at the temple, where they ask for a sign and misread his words about raising the temple as being about a building rather than his body. In Chapter 5 they object to a healed man carrying his mat on the Sabbath, then persecute Jesus and seek to kill him because he broke the Sabbath and called God his Father. In Chapter 6 they murmur at his claim to be the bread from heaven, pointing to his known parents, and argue among themselves. In Chapter 7 they look for him at the feast, marvel at his learning, and are so feared that no one speaks openly of him. In Chapter 8 many believe, but the group objects that they are Abraham's offspring, calls him a Samaritan with a demon, and takes up stones. In Chapter 9 they doubt the blind man's healing, question his parents, and declare Jesus a sinner. In Chapter 10 they are divided, press him to say if he is the Christ, and take up stones for blasphemy, claiming he, a man, makes himself God. In Chapter 11 some console Martha and Mary, and many who see Lazarus raised believe, while others report to the Pharisees. In Chapters 18 and 19 their officers seize and bind Jesus, take him to Annas and then Pilate, avoid defilement before Passover, state they may not put anyone to death, and choose Barabbas. They say by their law he must die for making himself the Son of God, press Pilate with the threat of Caesar, and ask that the crucified be removed before the Sabbath, after which Jesus is laid in a nearby tomb. Throughout, the group is divided in places, but its dominant force is opposition.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 2

At the temple the Jews ask Jesus what sign he shows for doing these things. When he says he will raise up the destroyed temple in three days, they object that it took forty-six years to build it and misunderstand that he speaks of his body.

Chapter 5

The Jews tell the healed man it is not lawful to carry his mat on the Sabbath and ask who told him to do so. Once told it was Jesus, they persecute him and seek all the more to kill him, because he broke the Sabbath and called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Jesus tells them they search the Scriptures but will not come to him for life, lack God's love, and receive glory from one another, and that Moses, on whom they set their hope, accuses them.

Chapter 6

The Jews murmur when Jesus says he is the bread that came down out of heaven, pointing out that they know his father and mother as the son of Joseph. They then contend with one another over how he can give his flesh to eat.

Chapter 7

The Jews seek to kill Jesus and look for him at the feast, asking where he is. They marvel at his learning and puzzle over his saying that they cannot come where he is, wondering if he will go to the Dispersion among the Greeks. People fear them, so no one speaks openly about Jesus.

Chapter 8

The Jews question Jesus' words about going away, and many of them believe in him after he speaks. Jesus tells those who had believed that remaining in his word makes them disciples, but they object that they are Abraham's offspring and never in bondage, and he says they seek to kill him. They accuse him of being a Samaritan with a demon, doubt that he has seen Abraham, and take up stones to throw at him.

Chapter 9

The Jews do not believe the man had been blind and received sight until they summon his parents. They had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus as Christ would be put out of the synagogue, which makes the parents afraid. They call the man a second time, tell him to give glory to God, and assert that Jesus is a sinner.

Chapter 10

The Jews are divided over Jesus' words, some saying he has a demon and is insane, others citing the opening of the blind's eyes. They press him to say plainly if he is the Christ, then take up stones to stone him for blasphemy because, as they say, he being a man makes himself God. They seek to seize him again but he goes out of their hand.

Chapter 11

Some of the Jews had recently tried to stone Jesus, and many come to console Martha and Mary. They weep, comment on Jesus' affection for Lazarus, and some ask why he who opened a blind man's eyes did not keep Lazarus from dying. Many who see the raising believe in him, but some go to the Pharisees and report what he did.

Chapter 18

The officers of the Jews seize and bind Jesus and lead him to Annas. They bring him to the Praetorium but do not enter, to avoid defilement before the Passover, tell Pilate it is illegal for them to put anyone to death, and shout for Barabbas, a robber, instead of Jesus.

Chapter 19

The Jews answer Pilate that by their law Jesus ought to die because he made himself the Son of God. They cry out that releasing him would make Pilate no friend of Caesar. They ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken so the bodies can be removed before the special Sabbath. Many of them read the title on the cross, and their Preparation Day leads to Jesus being laid in the nearby tomb.

Jews in The Acts of the Apostles

author unknown · the work’s page · read it where Jews first appears

Abstract written by a model

The Jews appear as a recurring body opposing Paul across his ministry. At Damascus, confounded by his proof that Jesus is the Christ, they plot to kill him, and he escapes. At Corinth they blaspheme, prompting him to turn to the Gentiles, and they bring him before Gallio, who dismisses them. Many thousands of Jews have believed and are zealous for the law, yet rumors say Paul teaches forsaking Moses; Asian Jews stir a crowd in the temple to kill him. Paul identifies himself as a Jew, born in Tarsus and zealous for God. They later join Tertullus's accusations before Felix, who, seeking their favor, leaves Paul in bonds.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter 9

The Jews of Damascus were confounded by Saul's proof that Jesus is the Christ, and after many days conspired to kill him, watching the gates day and night. Their plot became known to Saul, who escaped.

Chapter 18

At Corinth, the Jews oppose and blaspheme when Paul testifies that Jesus is the Christ, so he turns to the Gentiles. They rise up together against Paul and bring him before Gallio, who sends them away. At Ephesus they ask Paul to stay longer, and Apollos later refutes the Jews in Achaia.

Chapter 21

James and the elders note that many thousands of Jews have believed and are all zealous for the law, and that they have been told Paul teaches Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses. Other Jews, from Asia, stir up the multitude against Paul in the temple, and the crowd tries to kill him, fulfilling the prophecy that Jews would bind him.

Chapter 22

Jews in Damascus speak well of Ananias, and the Jews are those whom the commanding officer wants to understand as Paul's accusers. Paul presents himself as a Jew, born in Tarsus and zealous for God like his hearers.

Chapter 24

The Jews join in the attack on Paul, affirming Tertullus's accusations. Paul says certain Jews from Asia, who found him purified in the temple, ought to have appeared before Felix to accuse him. Felix, desiring to gain their favor, leaves Paul in bonds at the end.
